facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) is assumed for the adjoint and trace-class definitions and suppliers, and for the density expansion [F1]. No stronger choice principle is invoked.

facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] [[def-qft-finite-bounded-kraus-instrument]]: the outcome operators are $E_a=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$, the maps are $\mathcal J_a(X)=\sum_rM_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*$, and normalization means $\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_H$. The adjoint obeys $\langle Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,M^*y\rangle$.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]: under Countable Choice, a density operator is self-adjoint, positive and trace class with trace one, and has a trace-norm convergent expansion $\rho=\sum_jw_jT_{u_j,u_j}$ with $(u_j)$ orthonormal, $w_j\ge0$ and $\sum_jw_j=1$. We use statement (a); its separate statement (c) is not used.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[lem-nrqm-composites-nuclear-bounded-cyclicity]]: under Countable Choice, bounded multiplication of a nuclear representation gives trace-norm-convergent series for $BT$ and $TB$, with $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle$, $\operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle$, absolute convergence, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$. No unbounded factor is cyclically permuted.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]: $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ is trace class with $\|T_{u,v}\|_1=\|u\|\,\|v\|$ and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$; $T_{x,x}$ is self-adjoint and positive.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]: for bounded $B$, $BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v}$ and $T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v}$.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[def-trace-class-operator]]: a trace-class operator is in $\mathcal B(H)$ and has finite trace norm. [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]] defines the trace relative to a supplied Hilbert basis. [[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]] proves basis independence, linearity and $|\operatorname{tr}T|\le\|T\|_1$, hence continuity in trace norm.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]: positivity means that the quadratic-form values $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ are real and nonnegative; self-adjointness is the separate identity $T^*=T$.

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]: under Countable Choice, if $T$ is trace class and $A,B$ are bounded, then $ATB$ is trace class and $\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\|$.

facts.label: F8
facts.text: [F8] [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the Hilbert adjoint of every bounded operator $M$ is bounded, $\|M^*\|=\|M\|$, and $M^{**}=M$.

steps.text: For each $a,r$, $M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ is bounded by [F8]. Also [F8] gives $M_{a,r}^{**}=M_{a,r}$, so $\langle M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}x,y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}x,M_{a,r}^{**}y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}x,M_{a,r}y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}y\rangle$; hence it is self-adjoint. Its quadratic form is $\|M_{a,r}x\|^2\ge0$. Hence $E_a\ge0$. Normalization gives $I_H-E_a=\sum_{b\ne a}\sum_rM_{b,r}^*M_{b,r}\ge0$, including empty sums, so $E_a$ is an effect. [given, L1, F6, F8, algebra]

steps.text:
By [F8], each $M_{a,r}^*$ is bounded, so [F7] makes $M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*$ trace class; the finite sum $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is trace class. By [F8], $M_{a,r}^{**}=M_{a,r}$, and for all $x,y\in H$,
$\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,y\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}^*x,\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}^{**}\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle$,
where the first equality uses the adjoint identity for $M_{a,r}$, the second uses $\rho=\rho^*$, and the fourth uses the adjoint identity for $M_{a,r}^*$. Also $\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,x\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*x\rangle\ge0$. Finite summation shows $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is self-adjoint and positive. [given, A1, L1, F1, F6, F7, F8, algebra]
steps.claim:
By [F8], each $M_{a,r}^*$ is bounded, so [F7] makes $M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*$ trace class; the finite sum $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is trace class. By [F8], $M_{a,r}^{**}=M_{a,r}$, and for all $x,y\in H$,
$\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,y\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}^*x,\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}^{**}\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle$,
where the first equality uses the adjoint identity for $M_{a,r}$, the second uses $\rho=\rho^*$, and the fourth uses the adjoint identity for $M_{a,r}^*$. Also $\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,x\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*x\rangle\ge0$. Finite summation shows $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is self-adjoint and positive.

steps.text: By [F1], write $\rho=\sum_jw_jT_{u_j,u_j}$ in trace norm. For its partial sums $\rho_N=\sum_{j\le N}w_jT_{u_j,u_j}$, [F8] gives $\|M_{a,r}^*\|=\|M_{a,r}\|<\infty$, so [F7] gives $\|M_{a,r}(\rho-\rho_N)M_{a,r}^*\|_1\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|\rho-\rho_N\|_1\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\to0$. Thus [F4] gives $\mathcal J_a(\rho)=\sum_{r,j}w_jT_{M_{a,r}u_j,M_{a,r}u_j}$ in trace norm; the trace-norm sum is finite since $\sum_jw_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\le\|M_{a,r}\|^2\sum_jw_j=\|M_{a,r}\|^2$ for each $r$. Trace continuity [F5] and [F3] yield $p_a=\sum_{r,j}w_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\ge0$. Cyclicity [F2] gives $p_a=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\rho M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$. [given, A1, L1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, step 1.2, algebra]
steps.claim: By [F1], write $\rho=\sum_jw_jT_{u_j,u_j}$ in trace norm. For its partial sums $\rho_N=\sum_{j\le N}w_jT_{u_j,u_j}$, [F8] gives $\|M_{a,r}^*\|=\|M_{a,r}\|<\infty$, so [F7] gives $\|M_{a,r}(\rho-\rho_N)M_{a,r}^*\|_1\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|\rho-\rho_N\|_1\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\to0$. Thus [F4] gives $\mathcal J_a(\rho)=\sum_{r,j}w_jT_{M_{a,r}u_j,M_{a,r}u_j}$ in trace norm; the trace-norm sum is finite since $\sum_jw_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\le\|M_{a,r}\|^2\sum_jw_j=\|M_{a,r}\|^2$ for each $r$. Trace continuity [F5] and [F3] yield $p_a=\sum_{r,j}w_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\ge0$. Cyclicity [F2] gives $p_a=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\rho M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$.

steps.text: Because the outcome and Kraus index sets are finite, [F1] and step 2.1 give $\sum_ap_a=\sum_jw_j\langle(\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})u_j,u_j\rangle=\sum_jw_j\|u_j\|^2=1$ by normalization. Since every $p_a\ge0$, this also gives $p_a\le1$ for every $a$. [given, A1, L1, F1, step 2.1, algebra]

The finite sum $\sum_a\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is likewise positive trace class, and its trace is $\sum_ap_a=1$ by step 3.1, so it is a density operator. steps.text: For a unit vector $\psi$, [F3] gives that $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class with trace $\|\psi\|^2=1$, hence a density operator by [F1]. Also [F4] gives $M_{a,r}T_{\psi,\psi}M_{a,r}^*=T_{M_{a,r}\psi,M_{a,r}\psi}$. Taking traces and summing over the finite Kraus list yields $p_a=\sum_r\|M_{a,r}\psi\|^2$, as claimed. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the bounded linear operators on $H$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]); for $M\in\mathcal B(H)$, $M^*$ is its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,M^*y\rangle$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

A **finite bounded Kraus instrument datum** on $H$ consists of an integer $m\ge1$, integers $q_a\ge0$ for $a=1,\ldots,m$, and bounded operators $M_{a,r}\in\mathcal B(H)$ for $r=1,\ldots,q_a$. It is **normalized** when

$$\sum_{a=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_H.$$

Empty inner sums are zero. For each outcome $a$, define its outcome operator and operation by

$$E_a:=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad \mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*\quad(X\in\mathcal B(H)).$$

These formulas take values in $\mathcal B(H)$: each composition is bounded since $\|M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*x\|\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|X\|\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\,\|x\|$, and the sums are finite. This definition specifies only the displayed finite Kraus form; it is not a representation theorem for arbitrary instruments and does not assert that an apparatus realizes these data.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$
be a trace-class operator on $H$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $E$ be a
Hilbert basis of $H$, **supplied as data**
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]];
existence of such a basis is not asserted here). The **trace of $T$ relative to
$E$** is
$$\operatorname{tr}_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle,$$
the sum of the scalar family $(\langle Te,e\rangle)_{e\in E}$ in the
finite-subset-net sense of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

**The family is absolutely summable, uniformly in $E$.** Let
$T=\sum_js_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ be the singular-value series
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]],
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]) with
$(e_j)_{j\in J}$, $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ orthonormal and $\sum_js_j=\|T\|_1<+\infty$
([[def-trace-class-operator]]). For every $e\in H$ the series
$\langle Te,e\rangle=\sum_{j}s_j\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle$
converges absolutely, because the moduli are bounded by
$s_1\sum_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le s_1\|e\|^2$ by
Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[lem-finite-bessel-inequality]]). Consequently, for every finite
$F\subseteq E$, using the interchange of finite sums with the nonnegative
finite-subset supremum over $j$ and then finite Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel twice,
$$\sum_{e\in F}|\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\sum_{e\in F}\sum_{j}s_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|=\sum_{j}s_j\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le\sum_{j}s_j\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle f_j,e\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sum_{j}s_j=\|T\|_1 ,$$
because for each $j$ the two finite coefficient sums are bounded by
$\|e_j\|=1$ and $\|f_j\|=1$ (finite Bessel). Hence the finite subsums of
$|(\langle Te,e\rangle)|_{e\in E}$ are bounded by $\|T\|_1$, the family is
absolutely summable, and an absolutely summable family of scalars is summable in
ZF with $|\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\|T\|_1$
([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]). This justifies the
notation $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ before any basis-independence statement.

**Choice accounting and status.** Only a supplied basis $E$ and the singular
values of $T$ are used; no Hilbert basis of $H$ is assumed to exist, and the
next theorem proves that $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ does not depend on the
supplied basis and equals the basis-free trace of $T$
([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);

derivations.claim: For each $a,r$, $M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ is self-adjoint because $\langle M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}x,y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}x,M_{a,r}y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}y\rangle$, and its quadratic form is $\|M_{a,r}x\|^2\ge0$. Hence $E_a\ge0$. Normalization gives $I_H-E_a=\sum_{b\ne a}\sum_rM_{b,r}^*M_{b,r}\ge0$, including empty sums, so $E_a$ is an effect.

By [F7], each $M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*$ is trace class, so the finite sum $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is trace class. For all $x,y\in H$, $\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,y\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}^*x,\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle$ because $\rho=\rho^*$ and $M_{a,r}^*$ is the Hilbert adjoint. Also $\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,x\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*x\rangle\ge0$. Finite summation shows $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is self-adjoint and positive.

By [F1], write $\rho=\sum_jw_jT_{u_j,u_j}$ in trace norm. For its partial sums $\rho_N=\sum_{j\le N}w_jT_{u_j,u_j}$, [F7] gives $\|M_{a,r}(\rho-\rho_N)M_{a,r}^*\|_1\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|\rho-\rho_N\|_1\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\to0$. Thus [F4] gives $\mathcal J_a(\rho)=\sum_{r,j}w_jT_{M_{a,r}u_j,M_{a,r}u_j}$ in trace norm; the trace-norm sum is finite since $\sum_jw_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\le\|M_{a,r}\|^2\sum_jw_j=\|M_{a,r}\|^2$ for each $r$. Trace continuity [F5] and [F3] yield $p_a=\sum_{r,j}w_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\ge0$. Cyclicity [F2] gives $p_a=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\rho M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$.

Because the outcome and Kraus index sets are finite, [F1] and step 2.1 give $\sum_ap_a=\sum_jw_j\langle(\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})u_j,u_j\rangle=\sum_jw_j\|u_j\|^2=1$ by normalization. Since every $p_a\ge0$, this also gives $p_a\le1$ for every $a$.

If $p_a>0$, step 1.2 gives a positive trace-class numerator $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ and step 2.1 gives its trace $p_a$, so $\rho_a=\mathcal J_a(\rho)/p_a$ is positive trace class with trace one, hence a density operator by [F1]. The finite sum $\sum_a\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is likewise positive trace class, and its trace is $\sum_ap_a=1$ by step 3.1, so it is a density operator. If $p_a=0$, division by $p_a$ is undefined and no normalized update is asserted.

For a unit vector $\psi$, [F3] gives that $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class with trace $\|\psi\|^2=1$, hence a density operator by [F1]. Also [F4] gives $M_{a,r}T_{\psi,\psi}M_{a,r}^*=T_{M_{a,r}\psi,M_{a,r}\psi}$. Taking traces and summing over the finite Kraus list yields $p_a=\sum_r\|M_{a,r}\psi\|^2$, as claimed.

steps.text:
By [F4], $K$ is a Hilbert space, so its symmetric tensor sectors and
Fock space in the Statement are defined. Fix $k,m\ge0$, write $n=k+m$, and
let $\psi_m\in K_s^{(m)}$. Expanding
the permutation average and using symmetry of $\psi_m$ gives

placement $I$, the $k!m!$ permutations of the equal $e$ factors and the

steps.text: On a vector $e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m$ with $n=k+m$, creation by $e$ acts by $\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(e\otimes J_{k,m}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m))$. Since $P_{s,n+1}$ averages over all permutations, symmetrizing the last $n$ slots first does not change the result. This equals $\sqrt{n+1}\sqrt{\binom nk}P_{s,n+1}(e^{\otimes(k+1)}\otimes\psi_m)$. The binomial identity $\binom{n+1}{k+1}=\frac{n+1}{k+1}\binom nk$ makes this exactly $J_{k+1,m}(\sqrt{k+1}\,e^{\otimes(k+1)}\otimes\psi_m)$. Thus creation becomes the stated one-mode raising map. Annihilation by $e$ is zero for $k=0$, because every first tensor factor lies in $K$. Therefore $a(e)J_{k,m}\psi_m= \sqrt n\sqrt{\binom nk}\frac{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}{\binom nk} P_{s,n-1}(e^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\psi_m) =\sqrt k\,J_{k-1,m}\psi_m$, using $\binom nk=\frac nk\binom{n-1}{k-1}$. facts.label: A2
facts.text:
[A2] Set $X^0=\{\star\}$ with sigma-algebra $\{\varnothing,\{\star\}\}$
and unit mass $\mu_0(\{\star\})=1$. For one factor put
$\mathcal A_1=\mathcal A$ and $\mu_1=\mu$. For $n\ge2$, let
$\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$ be the recursively defined product sigma-algebra and
let $\mu_n$ be the completion of the $n$-fold product measure on it. Thus in
the Statement $\overline{\mu^{\times n}}$ means $\mu_n$ for $n\ge2$, and by
the one-factor base convention means $\mu$ for $n=1$; the vacuum component
uses $\mu_0$.

$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$. The map $\boldsymbol\omega$ is measurable from
$(X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathbb R^d,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d))$, and the PVM
$E$ in the Statement is indexed by $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$, as in
[[def-projection-valued-measure]].

sectors, with the second-variable-linear pairing fixed in

permutation projection in a completed Hilbert tensor power for $n\ge1$;

facts.label: F2
facts.text:
[F2] For $n\ge2$, the product-tensor unitary sends
$f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n$ to $\prod_{r=1}^n f_r(x_r)$; iteration
identifies the full tensor power with the full completed product $L^2$ space.
For $n=1$ the identification is the identity on $L^2(X,\mu)$.
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]

facts.label: F3
facts.text:
[F3] Coordinate permutations act unitarily, and the symmetric sector is the
range of their orthogonal averaging projection.
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]

facts.label: F4
facts.text:
[F4] For a densely defined operator, its adjoint is characterized by the
inner-product identity; a symmetric operator is self-adjoint exactly when its
domain equals the adjoint domain. Use the reversed-pairing form of the
definitions for the second-variable-linear convention.
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]

facts.label: F5
facts.text:
[F5] A core for a closed operator is a subspace of its domain dense for the
graph norm $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$.
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]]

facts.label: F6
facts.text:
[F6] Dominated convergence and Fatou's lemma apply on each measure space
$(X^n,\mu_n)$ and on the countable disjoint union $(\Omega,\mu_\Omega)$;
these integral theorems do not require the measure spaces to be complete.
[[thm-dominated-convergence]]
[[thm-fatou-lemma]]

facts.label: F7
facts.text:
[F7] The complex exponential satisfies $|e^{itq}|=1$ for real $t,q$ and
$e^{itq}e^{isq}=e^{i(t+s)q}$.
[[def-complex-exponential]]
[[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]

steps.text:
For $n\ge1$, each sector $H_s^{(n)}$ is a closed subspace of its Hilbert
tensor power, because it is the range of an orthogonal projection [F3]; the
zero-particle sector $H_s^{(0)}=\mathbb C$ is also complete. To prove that the
Fock direct sum is complete for arbitrary $H$, let $(\Psi^{(k)})_{k\ge1}$ be
Cauchy in its square-sum norm. Each coordinate is Cauchy in the complete
sector $H_s^{(n)}$, so it has a limit $\Psi_n$. A Cauchy sequence in a normed
space is bounded (its tail lies within distance $1$ of one fixed term, and
its finite initial segment is bounded); taking limits of each finite partial sum
$\sum_{n=0}^N\|\Psi_n^{(k)}\|^2$ shows
$\sup_N\sum_{n=0}^N\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty$, hence $\Psi=(\Psi_n)$ belongs to
the direct sum. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $K$ so that
$\|\Psi^{(k)}-\Psi^{(\ell)}\|\le\varepsilon$ for $k,\ell\ge K$; for fixed
$k\ge K$, take $\ell\to\infty$ in every finite coordinate sum to obtain
$\sum_{n=0}^N\|\Psi_n^{(k)}-\Psi_n\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ for every $N$.
Taking the supremum over $N$ proves $\Psi^{(k)}\to\Psi$. Truncating the
coordinate sequence proves that $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense.
For $n=1$ use the identity in [F2]. For $n\ge2$, iterate the product-tensor
unitary of [F2]; induction gives a unitary from $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ to
the full completed-product $L^2(X^n,\mu_n)$. On elementary tensors the
permutation $U_\pi$ becomes coordinate permutation, so by density the
unitary intertwines $P_{s,n}$ with averaging over coordinate permutations
[F3]. Its restriction identifies $H_s^{(n)}$ with the closed symmetric
subspace. Each $s_n$ is Borel measurable by [A3], since it is a finite sum
of measurable coordinate maps, and is invariant under all permutations.
The $n=0$ sector is $\mathbb C$ by definition. [A1, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

steps.text:
Let $\Omega=\bigsqcup_{n\ge0}X^n$ with the disjoint-union sigma-algebra and measure
$\mu_\Omega(C)=\sum_{n\ge0}\mu_n(C\cap X^n)$, using the conventions of [A2]; write $s_j$ for $s_{n,j}$ on component $n$. The Fock realization in step 1.1 is a closed subspace of $L^2(\Omega,\mu_\Omega)$ consisting of symmetric components. For $B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$, define $E(B)$ by multiplication by $\mathbf1_{s^{-1}(B)}$. Since $s$ is invariant under permutations, this multiplier preserves the symmetric subspace. It is an orthogonal projection because its multiplier is real and idempotent; $E(\varnothing)=0$, $E(\mathbb R^d)=I$ and $E(B)E(C)=E(B\cap C)$ follow pointwise. For pairwise disjoint $B_k\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ with union $B$, the squared norm of $E(B)\Psi-\sum_{k=0}^N E(B_k)\Psi$ is $$\sum_{n\ge0}\int_{X^n} \mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B\setminus\cup_{k=0}^N B_k)}|\Psi_n|^2\,d\mu_n.$$ The indicators tend pointwise to zero and the integrand is bounded by $|\Psi_n|^2$, whose total integral is $\|\Psi\|^2$; dominated convergence [F6] gives norm convergence. Hence $E$ is a strongly countably additive PVM on the Borel sets. [A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, given, construct]

steps.text: Fix a real measurable multiplier $f$ on $\Omega$ that is invariant under coordinate permutations, and define $M_f\Psi=f\Psi$ on the symmetric domain $D(M_f)=\{\Psi:f\Psi\in L^2(\Omega)\}$. This domain is dense: the symmetric cutoffs $\Psi\mathbf1_{|f|\le m}$ belong to it and converge in norm by dominated convergence. Reality of $f$ makes $M_f$ symmetric. If $\Psi\in D(M_f^*)$ and $K=M_f^*\Psi$, then for each $m$ the vector $v_m=(f\Psi-K)\mathbf1_{|f|\le m}$ is symmetric and lies in $D(M_f)$, since $f$ is bounded on its support. The adjoint identity gives $$0=\langle M_fv_m,\Psi\rangle_2-\langle v_m,K\rangle_2 =\int_{|f|\le m}|f\Psi-K|^2\,d\mu_\Omega.$$ Taking the union over $m$ shows $f\Psi=K$ almost everywhere, so $\Psi\in D(M_f)$ and $M_f^*\Psi=M_f\Psi$. Conversely, for every $\Psi\in D(M_f)$, reality of $f$ gives the adjoint identity against every domain vector, so $M_f^*\Psi=M_f\Psi$. Therefore $M_f$ is self-adjoint on its maximal multiplication domain. Apply this to $f=s_j$ to obtain each self-adjoint $H_j$, and to $f=\theta\cdot s$ to obtain $H_\theta$. [F4, F6, step 2.1, given, algebra]

steps.text: By [F6], $U_\theta(t)$ is unitary and $U_\theta(t+s)=U_\theta(t)U_\theta(s)$ on each component, including the vacuum where the phase is one. For any $\Psi$, the squared norm of $U_\theta(t)\Psi-U_\theta(t_0)\Psi$ is the integral over $\Omega$ of $|e^{it\theta\cdot s}-e^{it_0\theta\cdot s}|^2|\Psi|^2$; the integrand tends pointwise to zero and is bounded by $4|\Psi|^2$, so [F6] proves strong continuity. If $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, the pointwise difference quotient tends to $i(\theta\cdot s)\Psi$ and its squared error is bounded by $4|\theta\cdot s|^2|\Psi|^2$; dominated convergence proves norm convergence. Conversely, if the difference quotient has a norm limit as $t\to0$, take $t_m=1/m$. Fatou's lemma [F6] on the disjoint union gives $$\sum_n\int|\theta\cdot s_n|^2|\Psi_n|^2d\mu_n \le\liminf_m\left\|\frac{U_\theta(t_m)\Psi-\Psi}{t_m}\right\|^2<\infty,$$ so $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$; the forward calculation identifies the limit as $iH_\theta\Psi$. This proves the exact derivative criterion and all claims. [F6, F7, step 3.1, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$

graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is

facts.label: F1

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]: the operator $H_{\rm osc}$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $H_{\rm osc}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$.

facts.label: F11
facts.text: [F11] [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]: the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$.

facts.label: F12
facts.text: [F12] [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]: complex $L^2(\mathbb R)$ is complete for the integral pairing and its norm.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]]: $\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, with $g_{-1}=0$.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]: $\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ consists of smooth functions for which every polynomially weighted derivative is bounded; its functions and Fourier tests have rapidly decaying tails.

facts.label: F5
facts.text:
[F5] [[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]: $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(t)e^{-2\pi it\xi}\,dt$. The unnormalized positive-sign transform $\mathcal T_+\varphi(t)=\int e^{i
u t}\varphi(
u)\,d
u$ equals $\widehat\varphi(-t/(2\pi))$ after variable naming.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]]: the normalized Fourier transform maps $\mathcal S$ continuously to $\mathcal S$.

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: absolutely integrable product-space functions may be integrated in either order.

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; the oscillator and Fourier suppliers are invoked only under this stated axiom.

facts.label: F8

facts.label: F9
facts.text: [F9] [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]: the complex exponential is differentiable with derivative itself.

facts.label: F10
facts.text: [F10] [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]: $e^{ix}=\cos x+i\sin x$ and $|e^{ix}|=1$ for real $x$.

The function $\chi$ is even and integrable, $\psi(0)=0$, and $\psi(x)/x$ is bounded near zero because $\chi=1$ there and $\varphi$ is differentiable. Outside $[-1,1]$, $\psi=\varphi$, so $\psi(x)/x$ is integrable at infinity; on compact sets away from zero it is also integrable. For any integrable complex $q$, put $I=\int q$. If $I=0$, $|I|\le\int|q|$ is immediate; otherwise $\alpha=\overline I/|I|$ gives $|I|=\int\operatorname{Re}(\alpha q)\le\int|q|$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), $m_o>0$ in kilograms, $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $\hbar>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Take the complete oscillator family $(\psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ and self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H_{\rm osc}$ of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], with oscillator length $\ell=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_o\omega)}$ and $H_{\rm osc}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$. Let $\mathcal C=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n:n\ge0\}$ be the finite Hermite span. Multiplication by position $Xf(x)=xf(x)$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself by the Hermite recurrence. Define $U(t)$ on $\mathcal C$ by $U(t)\psi_n=e^{-i\omega(n+1/2)t}\psi_n$ and extend continuously to a unitary on the oscillator Hilbert space. For $\psi_0$ the normalized ground state, define
$$C_F(t)=\frac{m_o}{\hbar}\bigl(T X(t)X(0)\psi_0,\psi_0\bigr)_1,\qquad X(t)=U(t)^\dagger XU(t),$$
where time ordering means $T X(t)X(0)=X(t)X(0)$ for $t\ge0$ and $X(0)X(t)$ for $t<0$. Define $G_R(t)=1_{[0,\infty)}(t)\sin(\omega t)/\omega$.

Then, for every real $t$,
$$C_F(t)=\frac{e^{-i\omega|t|}}{2\omega},\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)C_F=-i\delta_0,\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)G_R=\delta_0.$$
The derivatives are distributional on $\mathbb R$, and $\delta_0(\varphi)=\varphi(0)$. Both kernels have units of seconds, so the differential identities have units of inverse seconds. In particular, $C_F(t)\ne0$ for $t<0$ while $G_R(t)=0$ there.

For a Schwartz test function $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and $\epsilon>0$, define $\operatorname{PV}\int\varphi(x)/x\,dx:=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\int_{|x|>r}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$ and $\delta_a(\varphi):=\varphi(a)$. The Plemelj boundary identity is
$$\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x+i\epsilon}\,dx =\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}x\,dx-i\pi\varphi(0),$$
with the opposite sign of $i\epsilon$ reversing the delta sign. In this boundary formula $x$ and $\epsilon$ use one common coordinate unit. For $\nu\in\mathbb R$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, the frequency regulator $\epsilon>0$ is in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and $\epsilon t$ is dimensionless; the ordinary positive-sign Fourier transform of $e^{-\epsilon|t|}C_F(t)$ is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\nu-\omega+i\epsilon}-\frac1{\nu+\omega-i\epsilon}\right).$$
As $\epsilon\downarrow0$ its distributional limit is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left[ \operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu-\omega}-\operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu+\omega} -i\pi\delta_{\omega}-i\pi\delta_{-\omega}\right],$$
which is conventionally denoted $i/(\nu^2-\omega^2+i0)$. Here that notation means the displayed pair of opposite boundary values at the two simple poles. This one-mode result makes no spatial-causality or interacting-field claim.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), $m_o>0$ in kilograms, $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $\hbar>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Take the complete oscillator family $(\psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ and self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H_{\rm osc}$ of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], with oscillator length $\ell=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_o\omega)}$ and $H_{\rm osc}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$. Let $\mathcal C=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n:n\ge0\}$ be the finite Hermite span. Multiplication by position $Xf(x)=xf(x)$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself by the Hermite recurrence. Define $U(t)$ on $\mathcal C$ by $U(t)\psi_n=e^{-i\omega(n+1/2)t}\psi_n$ and extend continuously to a unitary on the oscillator Hilbert space. For $\psi_0$ the normalized ground state, define
$$C_F(t)=\frac{m_o}{\hbar}\bigl(T X(t)X(0)\psi_0,\psi_0\bigr)_1,\qquad X(t)=U(t)^\dagger XU(t),$$
where time ordering means $T X(t)X(0)=X(t)X(0)$ for $t\ge0$ and $X(0)X(t)$ for $t<0$. Define $G_R(t)=1_{[0,\infty)}(t)\sin(\omega t)/\omega$.

Then, for every real $t$,
$$C_F(t)=\frac{e^{-i\omega|t|}}{2\omega},\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)C_F=-i\delta_0,\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)G_R=\delta_0.$$
The derivatives are distributional on $\mathbb R$, and $\delta_0(\varphi)=\varphi(0)$. Both kernels have units of seconds, so the differential identities have units of inverse seconds. In particular, $C_F(t)\ne0$ for $t<0$ while $G_R(t)=0$ there.

For a Schwartz test function $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and $\epsilon>0$, define $\operatorname{PV}\int\varphi(x)/x\,dx:=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\int_{|x|>r}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$ and $\delta_a(\varphi):=\varphi(a)$. The Plemelj boundary identity is
$$\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x+i\epsilon}\,dx =\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}x\,dx-i\pi\varphi(0),$$
with the opposite sign of $i\epsilon$ reversing the delta sign. In this boundary formula $x$ and $\epsilon$ use one common coordinate unit. For $\nu\in\mathbb R$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, the frequency regulator $\epsilon>0$ is in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and $\epsilon t$ is dimensionless; the ordinary positive-sign Fourier transform of $e^{-\epsilon|t|}C_F(t)$ is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\nu-\omega+i\epsilon}-\frac1{\nu+\omega-i\epsilon}\right).$$
As $\epsilon\downarrow0$ its distributional limit is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left[ \operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu-\omega}-\operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu+\omega} -i\pi\delta_{\omega}-i\pi\delta_{-\omega}\right],$$
which is conventionally denoted $i/(\nu^2-\omega^2+i0)$. Here that notation means the displayed pair of opposite boundary values at the two simple poles. This one-mode result makes no spatial-causality or interacting-field claim.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] The metric in the selected inertial basis is $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and the first basis vector $e_0$ is future unit timelike. [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] A proper orthochronous Lorentz map preserves $\eta_0$, has determinant $+1$, and preserves the chosen future timelike component; moreover these maps form a group under composition, including closure under inverse, by [[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]] and the definition in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]. In the selected inertial coordinates this is the group denoted $SO^+(1,3)$.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] The hyperbolic functions satisfy $\cosh^2\chi-\sinh^2\chi=1$, $\cosh$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$ on $[0,\infty)$, and $\sinh$ is odd and strictly increasing; the intermediate value theorem applies to real polynomials. [[def-hyperbolic-functions]] [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]] [[thm-intermediate-value]]

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] Every point $(a,b)$ with $a^2+b^2=1$ has the form $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ for some real $\theta$. [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] Cauchy--Schwarz gives $|\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_B|\le|\mathbf v|$ for unit $\mathbf n_B$. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] From the definitions, $\cosh\chi-\sinh\chi=\exp(-\chi)>0$. [[def-hyperbolic-functions]] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

steps.text: Let $u=\Lambda e_0=(u^0,\mathbf u)$. By [F1]–[F2], $u^0>0$ and $-(u^0)^2+|\mathbf u|^2=-1$, so $u^0=\sqrt{1+|\mathbf u|^2}$. If $\mathbf u=0$, then $u=e_0$; choose any unit spatial vector $\mathbf n_B$ and $\chi=0$, so $B_{\mathbf n_B}(0)=I$. Otherwise $\mathbf n_B=\mathbf u/|\mathbf u|$ is a unit vector and $u^0>1$. By the range and strict increase in [F3], there is a unique $\chi>0$ with $\cosh\chi=u^0$; then $\sinh\chi>0$ and $\sinh^2\chi=(u^0)^2-1=|\mathbf u|^2$, so $\sinh\chi=|\mathbf u|$. citations.quote:
An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] Countable Choice is the choice strength assumed for the completed Fock spaces. [[def-countable-choice]]

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] The Clifford matrices, $h_D$, $P_\pm$, particle and conjugate negative-energy subspaces, and the second-variable-linear pairing are those of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]. By [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], the matrix fields $P_\pm$ are bounded complementary orthogonal projections and their ranges $\mathcal H_\pm$ are closed separable Hilbert subspaces.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] The explicit $S_R,S_B$ obey $S\Gamma(p)S^{-1}=\Gamma(\Lambda p)$ and $S\beta S^\dagger=\beta$; each proper orthochronous $\Lambda$ factors into one boost and one rotation. [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]] [[lem-qft-lorentz-boost-rotation-factorization]]

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] The future mass shell is $p=(\omega(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)$ with $d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3 2\omega)$, and this measure is invariant under every proper orthochronous Lorentz map. [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] [[lem-qft-mass-shell-measure-invariant]]

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] The free Dirac field is the bounded smeared CAR field defined by $\Psi(F)=c(P_+u_F)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F})$; $F\mapsto u_F$ is continuous from Schwartz space to $\mathcal H_D$, and its separate positive and negative kernels are the Fourier distributions $C_+$ and $C_-$ displayed there, with tested pairings $\langle P_+u_F,P_+u_G\rangle$ and $\langle P_-u_F,P_-u_G\rangle$. [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]]

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] The antisymmetric Fock sectors, finite-particle domain, creation formulas, and CAR relations use the conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] and [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. By [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], $\mathcal H_\pm$ are separable, so their finite direct sum $\mathcal K=\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ is separable (take pairs from countable dense sets); with Countable Choice [A1], the hypotheses of the CAR supplier hold for $H=\mathcal K$.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] Smooth compactly supported vector functions are dense in $L^2$ on an open Euclidean set, componentwise. [[lem-smooth-compactly-supported-functions-are-dense-in-ltwo-of-an-open-set]]

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] The exact fermionic translation phases, maximal generator domains, joint PVM, forward-cone support, vacuum eigenspace and mass gap are established in [[lem-qft-dirac-fermionic-translation-spectrum]].

facts.label: F8
facts.text: [F8] In the fixed inertial coordinates of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], proper orthochronous Lorentz matrices satisfy $\Lambda^T\eta_0\Lambda=\eta_0$, have determinant $+1$, and preserve the chosen future cone, as defined in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]. The matrix group $SO^+(1,3)$ is closed under products and inverses by [[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

facts.label: F9
facts.text: [F9] The quarter-turn values give $\cos\pi=-1$, $\sin\pi=0$, $\cos2\pi=1$, and $\sin2\pi=0$. [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]

For translations the identities $S\Gamma(p)S^{-1}=\Gamma(\Lambda p)$ and $S eta S^\dagger= eta$ hold because $S=I$ and $\Lambda=I$. They hold for each explicit rotation and boost generator by [F2]. They are preserved under products: if they hold for $(\Lambda_1,S_1)$ and $(\Lambda_2,S_2)$, then $(S_2S_1)\Gamma(p)(S_2S_1)^{-1}=\Gamma(\Lambda_2\Lambda_1p)$ and $(S_2S_1) eta(S_2S_1)^\dagger= eta$. They are also preserved under inverses, since $S^{-1}\Gamma(r)S=\Gamma(\Lambda^{-1}r)$ follows by setting $p=\Lambda^{-1}r$ in the first identity, and $S^{-1} eta S^{-\dagger}= eta$ follows by multiplying the second identity by $S^{-1}$ and $S^{-\dagger}$. Thus both identities hold for every element of the subgroup $\widetilde G$ generated by the stated triples. Now for $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$ the projection identity in [F1] gives $P_+(\mathbf k) eta=(\Gamma(p)+\mu)/(2\omega)$. For $q=(\omega,-\mathbf k)$ it gives $P_-(\mathbf k) eta=(\Gamma(q)-\mu)/(2\omega)$. Thus, using $d
u_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3 2\omega)$, the separate kernels in [F4] are $$C_+(z)=\int(\Gamma(p)+\mu) eta e^{-ip\circ z}\,d
u_\mu(p),\qquad C_-(z)=\int(\Gamma(q)-\mu) eta e^{+iq\circ z}\,d
u_\mu(q),$$ where $p\circ z=p^0z^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf z$ and both $p,q$ range over the future mass shell. The matrix relations now established for every $	ilde g\in\widetilde G$, together with $S^{-1} eta= eta S^\dagger$, give $S(\Gamma(p)\pm\mu) eta S^\dagger=(\Gamma(\Lambda p)\pm\mu) eta$. In each shell integral, change variables $r=\Lambda p$ (or $r=\Lambda q$); invariance of $d
u_\mu$ [F3] and $(\Lambda p)\circ z=p\circ(\Lambda^{-1}z)$ show $C_\pm(\Lambda z)=S C_\pm(z)S^\dagger$. The coefficients grow at most linearly on the shell, so these Fourier integrals define tempered distributions and their pairings with Schwartz tests converge. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F8, algebra, construct]

steps.text: For $F,G\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C^4)$, [F4] identifies $\langle P_+u_F,P_+u_G\rangle$ and $\langle P_-u_F,P_-u_G\rangle$ with the respective kernel pairings $\int F(x)^\dagger C_\pm(x-y)G(y)\,d^4x\,d^4y$. Set $F'=\tau_{\tilde g}F$ and $G'=\tau_{\tilde g}G$. In each pairing, the spin factors are $S^{-1}$ and $S^{-\dagger}$; changing variables $x=a+\Lambda x'$, $y=a+\Lambda y'$ has unit Jacobian, cancels the translation in $x-y$, and the kernel identity of step 1.1 cancels both spin factors. Hence both polarized one-particle pairings are preserved, and the maps $P_\pm u_F\mapsto P_\pm u_{F'}$ are well-defined isometries on their test-generated subspaces. Applying the inverse group element proves they are onto after completion. For the conjugate negative-energy sector, conjugating the same preserved pairing and reversing its arguments gives the corresponding isometry on $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. steps.text: The test-generated subspaces are dense. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\};\mathbb C^4)$, $P_\pm u$ is smooth and compactly supported away from the massless apex; such projected vectors are dense in $\mathcal H_\pm$ by [F1] and [F6], since removing the single point does not change an $L^2$ class. Choose $g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\int g(t)dt=1$ and set $\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)=g(t)W_D(-t,\mathbf k)u(\mathbf k)$. This is smooth and compactly supported in $(t,\mathbf k)$; its inverse spatial Fourier transform is Schwartz by repeated integration by parts. The definition in [F4] then gives $u_F=u$, and hence $P_\pm u_F=P_\pm u$. [F1, F4, F6, step 1.1, construct]

steps.text: By steps 2.1 and 2.2 the particle and conjugate antiparticle test maps extend to unitaries on $\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. Their direct sum $T(\tilde g)$ is unitary. Define $U(\tilde g)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T(\tilde g)^{\otimes_a n}$ on the antisymmetric Fock sectors. Each tensor power is unitary by its isometric action on elementary tensors and inverse tensor power; it commutes with the signed permutation average and therefore restricts to a unitary on the antisymmetric sector. The direct sum is unitary and fixes $\Omega$. On elementary wedge tensors the insertion/contraction formulas of [F5] give $U c^\dagger(h)U^{-1}=c^\dagger(Th)$ and $U c(h)U^{-1}=c(Th)$; density extends these identities to the finite-particle domain. Thus $U(\tilde g)\Psi(F)U(\tilde g)^{-1}=\Psi(\tau_{\tilde g}F)$. Direct substitution in the affine and spinor formulas gives $\tau_{\tilde g_2}\tau_{\tilde g_1}=\tau_{\tilde g_2\tilde g_1}$: the coordinate argument is $(\Lambda_2\Lambda_1)^{-1}(x-a_2-\Lambda_2a_1)$ and the matrix factor is $(S_2S_1)^{-\dagger}=S_2^{-\dagger}S_1^{-\dagger}$. By [F8] the Lorentz factors compose within $SO^+(1,3)$; by the definition of $\widetilde G$ its triples are closed under this product. Hence $T$ and its Fock lift $U$ obey the same product law and $U$ is a representation. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

steps.text: The map $\tilde g\mapsto\tau_{\tilde g}F$ is continuous in Schwartz seminorms for each $F$, since it is composition with affine maps and finite matrices whose entries vary continuously. By the continuous test estimate of [F4], the one-particle representation is continuous on the dense test-generated subspaces of step 2.2; its operators have norm one, so approximation extends strong continuity to all one-particle vectors. On an elementary $n$-tensor, the difference of $T(g)^{\otimes n}$ and $T(g_0)^{\otimes n}$ is a sum of $n$ terms, each bounded by the norm of one factor difference times the norms of unchanged factors. It tends to zero as $g\to g_0$. Density and the unit norm bound extend this to each completed antisymmetric sector; finite-sector truncation then extends strong continuity to their direct sum. Applying $\Psi(F)^\dagger$ to $\Omega$ gives the particle component, and applying $\Psi(F)$ gives the antiparticle component. Products of these creation operators on $\Omega$ generate the algebraic antisymmetric tensors of their one-particle ranges; their span is dense in every sector by the definition of the Hilbert tensor completion.
