citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical scalar shell conventions of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and the second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Let $\mathcal H_D$ be the space of measurable functions $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^4$, modulo equality almost everywhere, with
$$\|u\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(\mathbf k)^\dagger u(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}<\infty,$$
and pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u(\mathbf k)^\dagger v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$. Define the measurable matrix $h_D(\mathbf k)=\sum_j\alpha_j k_j+\beta\mu$ and its maximal multiplication operator with domain $D(h_D)=\{u\in\mathcal H_D:h_Du\in\mathcal H_D\}$. For $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix fields
$$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=\frac12\left(I_4\pm\frac{h_D(\mathbf k)}{\omega(\mathbf k)}\right).$$
When $\mu=0$ at $\mathbf k=0$, set $P_+(0)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,0)$ and $P_-(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,I_2)$. These are complementary rank-two orthogonal projections; the value at this Lebesgue-null point does not change their multiplication operators. Write $M_{P_\pm}$ for their maximal multiplication operators and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}M_{P_\pm}$. The companion matrix lemma on this page proves these are bounded orthogonal projections with closed ranges. The conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ has vectors $\bar u$, scalar multiplication $z\bar u=\overline{\bar z u}$, and pairing $\langle\bar u,\bar v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$.

Use the sine and cosine definitions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. For a length-coordinate increment $t\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix multiplier
$$W_D(t,\mathbf k)=\cos(\omega t)I_4+i\frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega}h_D(\mathbf k).$$
At the massless apex set $W_D(t,0)=I_4$. Its unitarity, group law and generator identity are proved by the companion matrix lemma on this page.

The symbols $P_+$ and $P_-$ designate the positive- and negative-energy matrix formulas for this fixed free Dirac operator. This is purely mathematical data; no physical spin-statistics postulate or empirical assertion is included.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and use the definitions in [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]. For every $\mu\ge0$ and almost every $\mathbf k$, the displayed Pauli blocks satisfy $h_D(\mathbf k)^\dagger=h_D(\mathbf k)$, $h_D(\mathbf k)^2=\omega(\mathbf k)^2I_4$, and $P_\pm(\mathbf k)$ are complementary orthogonal projections of rank two. The ranges $\mathcal H_\pm$ are closed separable Hilbert subspaces of $\mathcal H_D$, and $h_D$ is self-adjoint on $D(h_D)=\{u:\omega u\in\mathcal H_D\}$. The matrices also satisfy $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ and $\gamma^{0\dagger}=\gamma^0$, $\gamma^{j\dagger}=-\gamma^j$.

For a unit spatial vector $\mathbf n$, put $\Sigma_{\mathbf n}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf n,\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf n)$, $S_R(\theta)=\cos(\theta/2)I_4-i\sin(\theta/2)\Sigma_{\mathbf n}$, and $S_B(\chi)=\cosh(\chi/2)I_4+\sinh(\chi/2)\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf n$. With $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$ the rotation $\mathbf v_\parallel+\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_\perp+\sin\theta\,\mathbf n\times\mathbf v_\perp$ using [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], with $\mathbf v_\parallel=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n$ and $\mathbf v_\perp=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_\parallel$, and $B_{\mathbf n}(\chi)$ the boost defined in [[lem-qft-lorentz-boost-rotation-factorization]], these matrices satisfy $S_R\Gamma(p)S_R^{-1}=\Gamma(R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)p)$, $S_B\Gamma(p)S_B^{-1}=\Gamma(B_{\mathbf n}(\chi)p)$, and $S_R\beta S_R^\dagger=S_B\beta S_B^\dagger=\beta$.

For each real $t$, $W_D(t,\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] is unitary, satisfies $W_D(t+s,\mathbf k)=W_D(t,\mathbf k)W_D(s,\mathbf k)$, and obeys $\partial_tW_D(t,\mathbf k)=i h_D(\mathbf k)W_D(t,\mathbf k)$.

Fix an inertial frame of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] and identify its vector coordinates with $\mathbb R^4$ and $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For a unit spatial vector $\mathbf n_B$ and $\chi\in\mathbb R$, define the boost $B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)$ by $B e_0=\cosh\chi\,e_0+\sinh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, $B\mathbf n_B=\sinh\chi\,e_0+\cosh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, and $Bw=w$ for every $w$ Euclidean-orthogonal to $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\mathbf n_B)$. Every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, as defined in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]], admits $\Lambda=B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$, where $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$ fixes the time axis and $\mathbf n_R$, and sends $\mathbf v_\perp$ to $\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_\perp+\sin\theta\,\mathbf n_R\times\mathbf v_\perp$ on the orthogonal plane, where $\mathbf v_\parallel=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_R)\mathbf n_R$ and $\mathbf v_\perp=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_\parallel$; the cross product is [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. If $\Lambda e_0=e_0$, choose $\chi=0$ and $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)=\Lambda$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

Assume Countable Choice. For every $\mu\ge0$, the measure $d\nu_\mu$ of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] is locally finite and sigma-finite on $H_\mu^+$.
For every proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$ and every
nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $H_\mu^+$,
$$\int_{H_\mu^+}g(\Lambda^{-1}p)\,d\nu_\mu(p) =\int_{H_\mu^+}g(p)\,d\nu_\mu(p).$$
The claim applies off the omitted apex when $\mu=0$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, and use [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], and the antisymmetric Fock and CAR conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] and [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. For $F\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C^4)$, define
$$\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}F(t,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x,\qquad u_F(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R}W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)\,dt.$$
Then $u_F\in\mathcal H_D$, continuously in the Schwartz topology, and
$$\Psi(F)=c(P_+u_F)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F})$$
defines a bounded operator on $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-})$, antilinear in $F$. It satisfies
$$\{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)\}=0,\qquad \{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)^\dagger\}=\langle u_F,u_G\rangle_{\mathcal H_D}I.$$
The positive and negative contraction kernels, defined as tempered distributions by their Fourier integrals, are
$$C_+(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{-i(\omega\tau-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_+(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3},\qquad C_-(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{+i(\omega\tau+\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_-(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}.$$
Their tested pairings give respectively $\langle P_+u_F,P_+u_G\rangle$ and $\langle P_-u_F,P_-u_G\rangle$; their sum is the anticommutator kernel $R$ below.
Its tested free equation is $u_{(i\partial_0-h_D(-i\nabla))F}=0$. For spatial Schwartz spinors $u,v$, the equal-time field $\Psi_t(u)=c(P_+W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u})$ satisfies $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)^\dagger\}=\int u(\mathbf x)^\dagger v(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x\,I$ and $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)\}=0$.

The spacetime anticommutator kernel is
$$R(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}W_D(-\tau,\mathbf k)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}=\partial_\tau\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x)I_4-i h_D(-i\nabla)\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x),$$
where $\Delta_\mu$ is the scalar causal commutator distribution of [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. Thus the kernel is supported in the closed causal cone. Spinor tests with compact spacelike-separated supports have vanishing anticommutators with one another and with each other's adjoints. Consequently, even polynomials in the bounded smeared fields commute across spacelike-separated regions. These are mathematical properties of the specified free-field construction.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and use [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] and [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]]. Define $\chi(s)=\cos s+i\sin s$ for real $s$, using [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. Let $X=(\{+\}\times\mathbb R^3)\sqcup(\{-\}\times\mathbb R^3)$ carry counting measure on the species label and $d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$ on each copy. The fiber $\mathcal V_x$ is $\mathbb C^4$ for $x=(+,\mathbf k)$ and $\overline{\mathbb C^4}$ for $x=(-,\mathbf k)$; $L^2(X;\mathcal V)$ denotes measurable sections with square-integrable fiber norm, and is the direct sum $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)\oplus L^2(\mathbb R^3;\overline{\mathbb C^4})$. Identify $\mathcal K=\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ with the closed subspace whose $+$ fibers lie in $\operatorname{ran}P_+(\mathbf k)$ and whose $-$ fibers lie in $\overline{\operatorname{ran}P_-(\mathbf k)}$; form its antisymmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$ using [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. For $x=(+,\mathbf k)$ set $q(x)=(\omega(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)$, and for $x=(-,\mathbf k)$ set $q(x)=(\omega(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. The one-particle translation multipliers $V(a)u(x)=\chi(q^0(x)a^0-\mathbf q(x)\cdot\mathbf a)u(x)$ preserve $\mathcal K$ and lift to a strongly continuous unitary representation on $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$. Write $U_j(t)$ for its Fock lift along the $j$th coordinate axis of $\mathbb R^4$.

On the $n$-particle sector, let $s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n q(x_r)$ and set $s_0=0$ on the vacuum sector. The joint spectral measure is multiplication by $\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}$ on each sector, restricted to its antisymmetric subspace. Its support is contained in the closed future cone $\{(E,\mathbf p):E\ge|\mathbf p|\}$. Define the time generator $H$ and spatial momentum components $P_j$ by $U(te_0)=\chi(tH)$ and $U(te_j)=\chi(-tP_j)$, where $e_\alpha$ are the coordinate vectors in translation space. Then $H$ and each $P_j$ are the maximal real multipliers by $s_{n,0}$ and $s_{n,j}$, respectively, with domains $\{\Psi:\sum_n\|s_{n,\alpha}\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$; the minus sign in spatial translation phases is the Minkowski pairing convention in $V(a)$. The vacuum is the unique zero-energy vector; for $\mu>0$ the nonvacuum spectrum has gap at least $\mu$, while for $\mu=0$ it has no positive gap.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] Assume Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] $P_T$ is an orthogonal projection of norm at most one and $\mathcal H_T$ is its closed range. [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] On finite-particle vectors, $[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I$ and the sector maps have bounds $\|a_n(h)\|\le\sqrt n\|h\|$, $\|a_n^\dagger(h)\|\le\sqrt{n+1}\|h\|$. [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] Bosonic Fock space is the square-summable direct sum of symmetric particle sectors, $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of vectors with only finitely many nonzero sectors, and the test class $C_c^\infty$ has its locally convex LF topology. [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]

steps.text: The integral in $g_j$ is the spacetime Fourier transform of a compactly supported smooth function, hence decreases faster than every inverse power of $|(\omega,\mathbf k)|$ by repeated integration by parts. Near $\mathbf k=0$, it is bounded by $\int|j|$, while the squared prefactor is $1/(2\omega)=1/(2|\mathbf k|)$. The radial integral of this bound is a constant times $\int_0^1r^2/r\,dr<\infty$. At infinity the rapid Fourier decay and $\|P_T\|\le1$ make the squared norm integrable. Also $P_Tg_j=g_j$ almost everywhere. Therefore $g_j\in\mathcal H_T$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

steps.text: By [F3], a vector in $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ has only finitely many nonzero sectors. On each such sector [F2] bounds creation and annihilation by the corresponding square-root particle number times $\|g_j\|\|\Psi_n\|$. Thus both maps and their sum are defined on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The same estimates bound every matrix element between fixed finite-particle vectors by a constant times $\|g_j\|$. On each fixed compact support, repeated integration by parts in step 1.1 bounds $\|g_j\|$ by finitely many smooth-test seminorms, so these matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology. This proves the asserted distributional smearing without defining a point field. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given]

steps.text:
Write $\omega=|\mathbf k|$, and use the Fourier convention $\widehat f(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(\mathbf x)e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d^3\mathbf x$. The expansion implied by the definition of $g_j$ is
$$A_i(x^0,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}}\left(a_i(\mathbf k)e^{-i\omega x^0+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}+a_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\right),$$
$$E_i(x^0,\mathbf x)=-\partial_0A_i(x^0,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(ia_i(\mathbf k)e^{-i\omega x^0+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}-ia_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\right).$$
Smearing the first line with $j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^3)$ gives exactly $a(g_j)+a^\dagger(g_j)$: the annihilation term uses conjugate-linearity of $a$, while the creation term is linear in its argument.
Here the formula is for $\mathbf k\ne0$; values at $\mathbf k=0$ are irrelevant to the integrals. The symbols $a_i(\mathbf k)$ and $a_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)$ are distributional notation for the Fock maps: for Schwartz vectors $u,v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^3$ set $a(u):=a(P_Tu)$ and $a^\dagger(v):=a^\dagger(P_Tv)$. Then [F2] gives $[a(u),a^\dagger(v)]=\int\overline{u_i(\mathbf k)}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)v_j(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k\,I$, equivalently the kernel notation $[a_i(\mathbf k),a_j^\dagger(\mathbf q)]=P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\delta^3(\mathbf k-\mathbf q)I$. The mode integrals are understood after test smearing; near $\mathbf k=0$ their squared one-particle weights behave respectively as $1/\omega$ and $\omega$, both locally integrable against $d^3\mathbf k$, and at infinity the Fourier transforms of the spatial tests decrease rapidly. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, given, algebra]

steps.text:
For real $f,h\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, define the equal-time spatial smearings by pairing the mode distributions with the spatial tests, $A(f):=\sum_i\int_{\mathbb R^3}f_i(\mathbf x)A_i(0,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x$ and $E(h):=\sum_j\int_{\mathbb R^3}h_j(\mathbf y)E_j(0,\mathbf y)\,d^3\mathbf y$. The one-particle vectors in these definitions are
$$g_f(\mathbf k)=\frac{P_T(\mathbf k)\widehat f(\mathbf k)}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}},\qquad e_h(\mathbf k)=-i\frac{\omega^{1/2}P_T(\mathbf k)\widehat h(\mathbf k)}{(2\pi)^{3/2}2^{1/2}}.$$
These belong to $\mathcal H_T$ by the preceding bounds, and $A(f)=a(g_f)+a^\dagger(g_f)$, $E(h)=a(e_h)+a^\dagger(e_h)$. The CCR [F2] gives
$$[A(f),E(h)]=-i\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}\,\overline{\widehat f_i(\mathbf k)}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\widehat h_j(\mathbf k)\,I.$$
For real $f,h$, this Fourier integral is real because $P_T$ is real and even and $\widehat f(-\mathbf k)=\overline{\widehat f(\mathbf k)}$, $\widehat h(-\mathbf k)=\overline{\widehat h(\mathbf k)}$.
Equivalently, as a tempered distribution in $\mathbf z=\mathbf x-\mathbf y$,
$$[A_i(0,\mathbf x),E_j(0,\mathbf y)]=-iK_{ij}(\mathbf x-\mathbf y),\qquad K_{ij}(\mathbf z)=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf z}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
The last integral defines a tempered distribution because $P_T$ is measurable and bounded: for $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$ its pairing is $(2\pi)^{-3}\int P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\widehat\varphi(-\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k$, which is absolutely convergent. Since the Fourier symbol of $P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla)$ is $P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)$, this distribution is exactly $P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)$. The sign is negative because $E=-\partial_0A$: the annihilation/creation cross terms contribute $-i/2$ each at equal time. Thus the stated equal-time commutator holds distributionally after smearing, with its stated sign. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, given] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

derivations.claim: The integral in $g_j$ is the spacetime Fourier transform of a compactly supported smooth function, hence decreases faster than every inverse power of $|(\omega,\mathbf k)|$ by repeated integration by parts. Near $\mathbf k=0$, it is bounded by $\int|j|$, while the squared prefactor is $1/(2\omega)=1/(2|\mathbf k|)$. The radial integral of this bound is a constant times $\int_0^1r^2/r\,dr<\infty$. At infinity the rapid Fourier decay and $\|P_T\|\le1$ make the squared norm integrable. Also $P_Tg_j=g_j$ almost everywhere. Therefore $g_j\in\mathcal H_T$.

By [F3], a vector in $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ has only finitely many nonzero sectors. On each such sector [F2] bounds creation and annihilation by the corresponding square-root particle number times $\|g_j\|\|\Psi_n\|$. Thus both maps and their sum are defined on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The same estimates bound every matrix element between fixed finite-particle vectors by a constant times $\|g_j\|$. On each fixed compact support, repeated integration by parts in step 1.1 bounds $\|g_j\|$ by finitely many smooth-test seminorms, so these matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology. This proves the asserted distributional smearing without defining a point field.

Apply the CCR [F2] to the positive- and negative-frequency terms of the mode expansion and use $E=-\partial_0A$. At equal time the two cross terms combine to
$$-i\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3} \left(\delta_{ij}-\frac{k_i k_j}{|\mathbf k|^2}\right)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)}.$$
This is the distributional Fourier multiplier $-iP_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)$; its action is defined by pairing the bounded multiplier against Schwartz tests. Thus the equal-time commutator holds after smearing, as claimed.

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] The normalized conventions give $D_a=\partial_a-iga_a$, $\mu=mc/\hbar$, $g=q\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$, and $A_a=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A)$ divided by $\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$. [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] For smooth commuting spinors, compact variations of the free density give the Euler equation $(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$ through the displayed first variation; the supplier fixes $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$. [[lem-qft-free-action-equations]]

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] The fixed representation has $\beta=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,-I_2)$, $\alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix}$ for Hermitian Pauli matrices $\sigma_j$, $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j$, and $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$. [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] The explicit block matrices of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] give $\beta^\dagger=\beta$, $\beta^2=I_4$, $\alpha_j^\dagger=\alpha_j$, and $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$; the last identity is checked by block multiplication in proof step 1.2.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] Assume Countable Choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

facts.label: A3
facts.text: [A3] The potential, spinor and real gauge parameter are smooth on the same open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, and every variation has compact support in $U$.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] Every open ball contains a nonnegative compactly supported smooth bump positive on a smaller ball. [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]

steps.text: Under $a\mapsto a+\partial\alpha$ and $\psi\mapsto e^{ig\alpha}\psi$, the chain rule gives $D'_a\psi'=e^{ig\alpha}D_a\psi$; the conjugate equation gives $D'_a\bar\psi'=e^{-ig\alpha}D_a\bar\psi$. The two phases cancel in each term of $\mathcal L_D$, so the density is gauge invariant. The explicit Countable Choice assumption is [A2]. [A1, A2, A3, given, algebra]
steps.claim: Under $a\mapsto a+\partial\alpha$ and $\psi\mapsto e^{ig\alpha}\psi$, the chain rule gives $D'_a\psi'=e^{ig\alpha}D_a\psi$; the conjugate equation gives $D'_a\bar\psi'=e^{-ig\alpha}D_a\bar\psi$. The two phases cancel in each term of $\mathcal L_D$, so the density is gauge invariant. The explicit Countable Choice assumption is [A2].

steps.text:
From [F2], $\beta=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,-I_2)$ is Hermitian and squares to $I_4$; each Pauli matrix is Hermitian, so $\alpha_j^\dagger=\alpha_j$, and the block formulas give $\alpha_j\beta=-\beta\alpha_j$. Therefore $(\gamma^0)^\dagger\beta=\beta^2=I_4=\beta\gamma^0$, while for $j=1,2,3$,
$$ (\gamma^j)^\dagger\beta=(\beta\alpha_j)^\dagger\beta=\alpha_j\beta^\dagger\beta=\alpha_j=\beta^2\alpha_j=\beta\gamma^j. $$
This proves [F3] from the exact matrix definitions. Now vary $\psi$ along a compactly supported complex $\chi$ and $\bar\psi$ along $\bar\chi$. Expanding the four kinetic terms and integrating the terms containing $D_a\chi$ or $D_a\bar\chi$ by parts gives
$$\delta S_D=2\operatorname{Re}\int_U\chi^\dagger\beta R_D\,d^4x, \qquad R_D=(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi.$$
For example, $\int\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\chi=-\int(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\chi$ and $-\int(D_a\bar\chi)\gamma^a\psi=\int\bar\chi\gamma^aD_a\psi$; compact support removes both boundary terms. The resulting variation is
$$i\int\bigl(\bar\chi\gamma^aD_a\psi-(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\chi\bigr)d^4x-\mu\int(\bar\chi\psi+\bar\psi\chi)d^4x =\int\bigl(\bar\chi R_D+\overline{\bar\chi R_D}\bigr)d^4x,$$
where the equality uses $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$ from [F3]. If $R_D(x_0)\ne0$, continuity and openness of $U$ give a ball contained in $U$ where $|R_D|>0$; choose a bump $\rho$ from [F4] there and take $\chi=\rho\beta R_D$. Since $\beta^\dagger\beta=I_4$, this gives $\delta S_D=2\int\rho|R_D|^2d^4x>0$, contradicting stationarity. Thus stationarity is equivalent to $R_D=0$ pointwise, and taking the adjoint gives $-i(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a-\mu\bar\psi=0$. This is the charged version of the compact-variation identity in [F1]; the additional $a_a$ terms are smooth multiplication terms. [A1, A2, A3, F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

steps.text:
Contract the first equation in step 1.2 on the left by $\bar\psi$ and the adjoint equation on the right by $\psi$. Subtracting cancels the equal mass terms and gives
$$i\bigl(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi+(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\bigr)=0.$$
The parenthesis equals $\partial_a(\bar\psi\gamma^a\psi)$ because the $+ig a_a\bar\psi$ and $-ig a_a\psi$ contributions cancel. Since $i\ne0$ and $g$ is constant, $\partial_a j^a=0$. [step 1.2, F2, given, algebra]

Use the fixed Minkowski coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)=(ct,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, on an open coordinate domain $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ with its standard topology. Each $x^a$ has unit metre. For a smooth scalar component $u:U\to\mathbb R$ or $u:U\to\mathbb C$, define $\partial_a u:=\partial u/\partial x^a$; thus $\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t$ at fixed $\mathbf x$, $\partial_j=\partial/\partial x^j$ for $j=1,2,3$, and each $\partial_a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Raise derivative indices with $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$. The fields in this definition are smooth maps
$$\phi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathbf A\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R^3),\qquad \psi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4),\qquad \chi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R).$$
Define the lower-potential component maps $A_a:U\to\mathbb R$ by $A_0=-\phi/c$ and $A_j=\mathbf A_j$; collectively $(A_a)$ is the real covector potential in this chart. Then $F_{ab}:=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ has smooth real component maps $F_{ab}:U\to\mathbb R$. The spinor is an ordinary commuting $\mathbb C^4$-valued map, not a tuple of Grassmann generators. Its Dirac adjoint is the smooth row-valued map $\bar\psi:=\psi^\dagger\beta:U\to(\mathbb C^4)^*$, using the fixed matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], so $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$. In fixed SI units, $\phi$ is in volts, each $A_a$ is in $\mathrm{T\,m}$, $\psi$ is assigned field dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$, and $\chi$ is in webers; these unit labels accompany the maps and do not identify $q$ with a measured charge. For periodic spatial domains, the same component and unit conventions apply to smooth periodic coordinate lifts, with the quotient domain specified by the item using them.

For the SI-normalization bookkeeping, let $c>0$ (m s$^{-1}$), $\hbar>0$ (J s), $\mu_0>0$ (N A$^{-2}$), a real charge parameter $q$ (C), and a mass parameter $m>0$ (kg) be symbolic inputs; put $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. In the current SI, $c$ and $h$ are defining constants while $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined; the formula below keeps $\mu_0$ symbolic and assigns it no numerical value. Use the lower-potential convention
$$A_a=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A),$$
where $A_a$ has units T m, $\phi$ is in volts, and $\mathbf A$ is in T m. Define
$$S_0=\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c},\qquad a_a=A_a/S_0,\qquad f_{ab}=\partial_aa_b-\partial_ba_a,$$
$$\mu=mc/\hbar,\qquad g=q\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}=q/\sqrt{\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad D_a=\partial_a-ig a_a.$$
Here $D_a$ acts on $\psi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4)$ by $(D_a\psi)(x)=\partial_a\psi(x)-ig a_a(x)\psi(x)$, again a smooth map $U\to\mathbb C^4$. Thus $a_a$ and $\mu$ have units m$^{-1}$, $f_{ab}$ has units m$^{-2}$, and $g$ is dimensionless. For $\psi$ with units m$^{-3/2}$, both $-\tfrac14 f_{ab}f^{ab}$ and $\bar\psi(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi$ have units m$^{-4}$; their integral over $d^4x$ is dimensionless and represents the action divided by $\hbar$ in this normalization.

For the real smooth gauge-parameter map $\chi:U\to\mathbb R$ in webers, put $\alpha:=\chi/S_0\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ (dimensionless) and use
$$A'_a=A_a+\partial_a\chi,\qquad a'_a=a_a+\partial_a\alpha,\qquad \psi'=e^{ig\alpha}\psi.$$
The induced covariant derivative is $D'_a=\partial_a-ig a'_a$. These are formal mathematical conventions for the later conditional deductions. They do not adopt a measured value of $\mu_0$, identify $q$ with an electron charge, impose charge quantization, or assert that interacting continuum fields exist.

Fix $\mu\ge0$, $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\Box=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$, and the Dirac matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]; $\mu$ is the inverse-length mathematical shell parameter of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. For a smooth real scalar field $\phi$ and smooth commuting complex spinor $\psi:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb C^4$, use the normalized free Lagrangian densities
$$\mathcal L_\phi=-\frac12\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi\,\partial_b\phi+\mu^2\phi^2\right),\qquad \mathcal L_D=\bar\psi\left(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu\right)\psi,\qquad \bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta.$$
For compactly supported smooth real variations $h$ and compactly supported smooth complex spinor variations $\chi$, the action symbols are used only through the following finite, compactly supported first variations; no global integrability of the background fields is assumed:
$$\delta S_\phi(\phi;h)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h(\Box-\mu^2)\phi\,d^4x,\qquad \delta S_D(\psi;\chi)=2\operatorname{Re}\int_{\mathbb R^4}\chi^\dagger\beta\left(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu\right)\psi\,d^4x.$$
Each field is stationary under all such variations if and only if its corresponding Euler–Lagrange equation holds pointwise:
$$(\Box-\mu^2)\phi=0,\qquad (i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0.$$
The adjoint Dirac equation follows from the second equation because the fixed matrices satisfy $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$. These are mathematical variation identities for commuting classical fields; they assert no quantization, Grassmann calculus, or physical measurement.

The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Let $\mathcal H_D$ be the space of measurable functions $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^4$, modulo equality almost everywhere, with
$$\|u\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(\mathbf k)^\dagger u(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}<\infty,$$
and pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u(\mathbf k)^\dagger v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$. Define the measurable matrix $h_D(\mathbf k)=\sum_j\alpha_j k_j+\beta\mu$ and its maximal multiplication operator with domain $D(h_D)=\{u\in\mathcal H_D:h_Du\in\mathcal H_D\}$. $$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=\frac12\left(I_4\pm\frac{h_D(\mathbf k)}{\omega(\mathbf k)}\right).$$
When $\mu=0$ at $\mathbf k=0$, set $P_+(0)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,0)$ and $P_-(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,I_2)$. These are complementary rank-two orthogonal projections; the value at this Lebesgue-null point does not change their multiplication operators. Write $M_{P_\pm}$ for their maximal multiplication operators and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}M_{P_\pm}$. The companion matrix lemma on this page proves these are bounded orthogonal projections with closed ranges. The conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ has vectors $\bar u$, scalar multiplication $z\bar u=\overline{\bar z u}$, and pairing $\langle\bar u,\bar v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$.

Use the sine and cosine definitions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. For a length-coordinate increment $t\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix multiplier
$$W_D(t,\mathbf k)=\cos(\omega t)I_4+i\frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega}h_D(\mathbf k).$$
At the massless apex set $W_D(t,0)=I_4$. Its unitarity, group law and generator identity are proved by the companion matrix lemma on this page.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: Under $a\mapsto a+\partial\alpha$ and $\psi\mapsto e^{ig\alpha}\psi$, the chain rule gives $D'_a\psi'=e^{ig\alpha}D_a\psi$; the conjugate equation gives $D'_a\bar\psi'=e^{-ig\alpha}D_a\bar\psi$. The two phases cancel in each term of $\mathcal L_D$, so the density is gauge invariant. The explicit Countable Choice assumption is [A2].

From [F2], $\beta=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,-I_2)$ is Hermitian and squares to $I_4$; each Pauli matrix is Hermitian, so $\alpha_j^\dagger=\alpha_j$, and the block formulas give $\alpha_j\beta=-\beta\alpha_j$. Therefore $(\gamma^0)^\dagger\beta=\beta^2=I_4=\beta\gamma^0$, while for $j=1,2,3$,
$$ (\gamma^j)^\dagger\beta=(\beta\alpha_j)^\dagger\beta=\alpha_j\beta^\dagger\beta=\alpha_j=\beta^2\alpha_j=\beta\gamma^j. $$
This proves [F3] from the exact matrix definitions. Now vary $\psi$ along a compactly supported complex $\chi$ and $\bar\psi$ along $\bar\chi$. Expanding the four kinetic terms and integrating the terms containing $D_a\chi$ or $D_a\bar\chi$ by parts gives
$$\delta S_D=2\operatorname{Re}\int_U\chi^\dagger\beta R_D\,d^4x, \qquad R_D=(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi.$$
For example, $\int\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\chi=-\int(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\chi$ and $-\int(D_a\bar\chi)\gamma^a\psi=\int\bar\chi\gamma^aD_a\psi$; compact support removes both boundary terms. The resulting variation is
$$i\int\bigl(\bar\chi\gamma^aD_a\psi-(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\chi\bigr)d^4x-\mu\int(\bar\chi\psi+\bar\psi\chi)d^4x =\int\bigl(\bar\chi R_D+\overline{\bar\chi R_D}\bigr)d^4x,$$
where the equality uses $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$ from [F3]. If $R_D(x_0)\ne0$, continuity and openness of $U$ give a ball contained in $U$ where $|R_D|>0$; choose a bump $\rho$ from [F4] there and take $\chi=\rho\beta R_D$. Since $\beta^\dagger\beta=I_4$, this gives $\delta S_D=2\int\rho|R_D|^2d^4x>0$, contradicting stationarity. Thus stationarity is equivalent to $R_D=0$ pointwise, and taking the adjoint gives $-i(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a-\mu\bar\psi=0$. This is the charged version of the compact-variation identity in [F1]; the additional $a_a$ terms are smooth multiplication terms.

Contract the first equation in step 1.2 on the left by $\bar\psi$ and the adjoint equation on the right by $\psi$. Subtracting cancels the equal mass terms and gives

steps.text: Integrating this equation over the periodic box at any fixed $t$ gives $0=L^{-3}\int(-\Delta\phi)\,d^3\mathbf x=L^{-3}\epsilon_0^{-1}\int\rho\,d^3\mathbf x$, since each periodic first derivative has equal boundary values on opposite faces. Thus neutrality is necessary at each time. For neutral data, fix a compact interval $K\subset I$ and integers $r,M\ge0$. Differentiating the Fourier coefficient under the integral gives $\partial_t^r\widehat\rho_k(t)=L^{-3}\int_{[0,L]^3}\partial_t^r\rho(\mathbf x,t)e^{-2\pi i k\cdot\mathbf x/L}\,d^3\mathbf x$. For $k\ne0$, repeated periodic integration by parts $M$ times in a coordinate $j$ with $|k_j|\ge|k|/\sqrt3$ gives $|\partial_t^r\widehat\rho_k(t)|\le C_{r,M,K}(1+|k|)^{-M}$ uniformly for $t\in K$; boundedness of the finitely many low modes is absorbed in the constant. Since $\widehat\phi_k=\widehat\rho_k/(\epsilon_0|2\pi k/L|^2)$ for $k\ne0$, a mixed derivative $\partial_t^r\partial_{\mathbf x}^{\alpha}$ of its Fourier series is bounded termwise on $K\times T_L^3$ by a constant times $|k|^{|\alpha|-M-2}$. For the SI-normalization bookkeeping, let $c>0$ (m s$^{-1}$), $\hbar>0$ (J s), $\mu_0>0$ (N A$^{-2}$), a real charge parameter $q$ (C), and a mass parameter $m>0$ (kg) be symbolic inputs; put $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. In the current SI, $c$ and $h$ are defining constants while $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined; the formula below keeps $\mu_0$ symbolic and assigns it no numerical value. $$A_a=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A),\qquad F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a,$$
where $A_a$ has units T m, $\phi$ is in volts, and $\mathbf A$ is in T m. Define
$$S_0=\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c},\qquad a_a=A_a/S_0,\qquad f_{ab}=\partial_aa_b-\partial_ba_a,$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], and use [[def-qft-example-data]] and [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. A proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map is a real linear $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda$ preserving the future cone $E>0$. For future energy four-vectors in the algebraic metric $h=(+,-,-,-)$, the shell measure $d^3\mathbf p/((2\pi)^3\,2E)$ is invariant under every such map. Write $E_i(r)=\sqrt{r^2+\mathsf M_i^2}$. Let $f$ be a nonnegative Borel function on the product of the positive shells of [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. The standard two-body on-shell integral
$$(2\pi)^4\int d\nu_{\mathsf M_1}(k_1)d\nu_{\mathsf M_2}(k_2)\, \delta^{(4)}(P-k_1-k_2)\,f(k_1,k_2)$$
is interpreted by first evaluating the spatial delta in $k_2$, then the one-dimensional energy delta by the increasing radial change of variable $r\mapsto E_1(r)+E_2(r)$. Explicitly, after the spatial evaluation its radial action is $\int_0^\infty g(r)\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r))\,dr=g(k_*)/(d(E_1+E_2)/dr|_{k_*})$ for nonnegative Borel $g$; this is the pushforward evaluation under that $C^1$ diffeomorphism, not a product of distributions. It equals $\int f\,d\Phi_2$ from the Definition. The threshold root is $k_*$ in that Definition, and
$$\int d\Phi_2=\frac{k_*}{4\pi\sqrt{s}}.$$
For equal rest energies $\mathsf M_1=\mathsf M_2=\mathsf M$, set $\beta=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/s}$; then $k_*=\sqrt{s}\beta/2$ and $\int d\Phi_2=\beta/(8\pi)$. For future incoming energy four-vectors $p_1,p_2$ with $p_1+p_2=P$ and nonnegative rest energies $\mathsf M_{1,\mathrm{in}},\mathsf M_{2,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, let $p_*$ be their center-of-momentum spatial momentum magnitude. Their invariant flux is $F=4p_*\sqrt{s}$. For equal incoming rest energies $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}\geq0$ with $s\geq4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$, define $\beta_{\mathrm{in}}=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2/s}$; then $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. For finite nonempty incoming and outgoing label sets, normalized initial weights, and the Borel amplitude family of the Definition, whenever $F>0$ the cross-section coefficient map gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{64\pi^2s}\, \frac{k_*}{p_*}\, \frac{\overline{|\mathcal A|^2}}{S_f}.$$
For a parent at rest with energy $\mathsf M_0>2\mathsf M$ decaying to two equal rest-energy daughters with constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is $|G_E|^2\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/\mathsf M_0^2}/(32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0)$ when the daughters are identical. This is a coefficient calculation, not a claim of exponential survival.

Let $m\geq0$ be a scalar rest energy in joules and $s>4m^2$. For one scalar initial label of weight $1$ and one specified final channel, take the dimensionless real quartic tree amplitude $\mathcal A=-\lambda$. The coefficient map of [[lem-qft-example-two-body-phase-space]] gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{\lambda^2(\hbar c)^2}{128\pi^2s}, \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}=\frac{\lambda^2(\hbar c)^2}{32\pi s}$$
for identical final scalars integrated over the full labeled sphere. For distinguishable final scalars the two coefficients are twice these values.

For a parent at rest with energy $\mathsf M_0>2m$ decaying through a specified single channel to two identical scalars of rest energy $m$ under a constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is
$$\Gamma_{\mathrm{coeff}} =\frac{|G_E|^2}{32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0} \sqrt{1-\frac{4m^2}{\mathsf M_0^2}}.$$
This result concerns the defined formal coefficients. It does not assert an exact exponential survival law.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], and use [[def-qft-example-data]] and [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. A proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map is a real linear $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda$ preserving the future cone $E>0$. For future energy four-vectors in the algebraic metric $h=(+,-,-,-)$, the shell measure $d^3\mathbf p/((2\pi)^3\,2E)$ is invariant under every such map. Write $E_i(r)=\sqrt{r^2+\mathsf M_i^2}$. Let $f$ be a nonnegative Borel function on the product of the positive shells of [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. The standard two-body on-shell integral
$$(2\pi)^4\int d\nu_{\mathsf M_1}(k_1)d\nu_{\mathsf M_2}(k_2)\, \delta^{(4)}(P-k_1-k_2)\,f(k_1,k_2)$$
is interpreted by first evaluating the spatial delta in $k_2$, then the one-dimensional energy delta by the increasing radial change of variable $r\mapsto E_1(r)+E_2(r)$. Explicitly, after the spatial evaluation its radial action is $\int_0^\infty g(r)\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r))\,dr=g(k_*)/(d(E_1+E_2)/dr|_{k_*})$ for nonnegative Borel $g$; this is the pushforward evaluation under that $C^1$ diffeomorphism, not a product of distributions. It equals $\int f\,d\Phi_2$ from the Definition. The threshold root is $k_*$ in that Definition, and
$$\int d\Phi_2=\frac{k_*}{4\pi\sqrt{s}}.$$
For equal rest energies $\mathsf M_1=\mathsf M_2=\mathsf M$, set $\beta=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/s}$; then $k_*=\sqrt{s}\beta/2$ and $\int d\Phi_2=\beta/(8\pi)$. For future incoming energy four-vectors $p_1,p_2$ with $p_1+p_2=P$ and nonnegative rest energies $\mathsf M_{1,\mathrm{in}},\mathsf M_{2,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, let $p_*$ be their center-of-momentum spatial momentum magnitude. Their invariant flux is $F=4p_*\sqrt{s}$. For equal incoming rest energies $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}\geq0$ with $s\geq4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$, define $\beta_{\mathrm{in}}=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2/s}$; then $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. For finite nonempty incoming and outgoing label sets, normalized initial weights, and the Borel amplitude family of the Definition, whenever $F>0$ the cross-section coefficient map gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{64\pi^2s}\, \frac{k_*}{p_*}\, \frac{\overline{|\mathcal A|^2}}{S_f}.$$
For a parent at rest with energy $\mathsf M_0>2\mathsf M$ decaying to two equal rest-energy daughters with constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is $|G_E|^2\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/\mathsf M_0^2}/(32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0)$ when the daughters are identical. This is a coefficient calculation, not a claim of exponential survival.

facts.label: F2
facts.text:
[F2] [[lem-qft-example-four-dimensional-radial-measure]]: for every
nonnegative Borel radial function on a closed radius-$\Lambda$ ball in
$\mathbb R^4$, the radial measure is $2\pi^2r^3\,dr$.

facts.label: F3
facts.text:
[F3] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: the integral of a continuous derivative on a
closed bounded interval is the difference of its endpoint values.

facts.label: F4
facts.text:
[F4] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: for $u>0$,
$\log u$ has derivative $1/u$ and is the integral of $1/u$ between positive
endpoints.

facts.label: F5
facts.text:
[F5] [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]: the positive
exponential is the real restriction of the complex power series ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]), which converges everywhere; all terms are nonnegative for real $y\ge0$, so
$e^y\ge y^n/n!$ for $y\ge0$ and each integer $n\ge0$.

facts.label: F6
F7
facts.text:
[F7] Integration by parts on a closed interval applies to differentiable
real functions with integrable derivatives; in particular it applies to
continuously differentiable functions.
[[thm-integration-by-parts]]

facts.label: F8
facts.text:
[F8] Integer powers are differentiable with $(x^n)'=nx^{n-1}$ for
$n\ge1$. [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]]

facts.label: F9
facts.text:
[F9] Under Countable Choice, bounded Riemann-integrable real functions on
compact intervals have the same Lebesgue integrals; nonnegative functions
Riemann integrable on every compact half-line interval with a finite improper
Riemann limit have the same half-line Lebesgue integral.
[[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]],
[[thm-nonnegative-improper-riemann-integral-agrees-with-the-lebesgue-integral-on-a-half-line]]

steps.text:
The integrand $r\mapsto r^3/(r^2+\mu^2)$ is nonnegative and continuous on
$[0,\Lambda]$. Apply [F2], then divide by $(2\pi)^4$, to obtain
$$ I_\Lambda=\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_0^\Lambda \frac{r^3}{r^2+\mu^2}\,dr. $$
Polynomial division gives
$r^3/(r^2+\mu^2)=r-\mu^2r/(r^2+\mu^2)$. By [F4], an antiderivative is
$G(r)=r^2/2-(\mu^2/2)\log(r^2+\mu^2)$ on this interval. Its derivative is
continuous; its compact-interval integrands are bounded and Riemann integrable, so [F9] identifies their Lebesgue integrals with the calculus integrals. Thus [F3] evaluates the integral as
$$ G(\Lambda)-G(0) =\frac12\left(\Lambda^2-\mu^2\log(1+\Lambda^2/\mu^2)\right). $$
Multiplying by $1/(8\pi^2)$ gives the claimed expression. [given, A1, F2,
F3, F4, F9, algebra]

By [F6], $-e^{-x}$ has derivative $e^{-x}$; [F3] on $[0,R]$
gives $\int_0^R e^{-x}dx=1-e^{-R}$. The positive series [F5] gives
$e^R\ge1+R$, so $e^{-R}\to0$ and $M_0=1$.
For each integer $n\ge0$, [F5] with $y=x/2$ gives
$x^ne^{-x}\le2^n n!e^{-x/2}$. The majorant has finite integral $2^{n+1}n!$
by [F3] and [F6]; the positive truncated integrals are increasing and bounded by this finite integral, hence have a finite improper limit. All the integrands are continuous on every compact interval; [F9] identifies these convergent nonnegative improper integrals with their half-line Lebesgue integrals. Thus $M_n=\int_0^\infty x^ne^{-x}dx$ is finite.
The same bound and $e^{x/2}\ge1+x/2$ show $x^ne^{-x}\to0$.
For $n\ge1$ and $R>0$, take $u(x)=x^n$, $v(x)=-e^{-x}$ on $[0,R]$.
They are continuously differentiable with continuous, hence integrable,
derivatives. Thus [F7] gives
$$\int_0^R x^ne^{-x}dx=-R^ne^{-R}+n\int_0^R x^{n-1}e^{-x}dx.$$
The endpoint at zero vanishes since $n\ge1$. Taking $R\to\infty$ is
justified by the finite positive improper integrals and the vanishing
boundary term just proved. It gives $M_n=nM_{n-1}$, and induction from

$0\le e^{-x}/(1+\lambda x)\le e^{-x}$ for $\lambda\ge0$, so $F(\lambda)$
is finite. [given, A1, F3, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, algebra]
