This is a classical conditional solver for smooth periodic neutral data; it makes no claim about quantum density products or nonperiodic boundary conditions.

Assume Countable Choice, the constants in [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]], $\hbar>0$, and a finite integer $N\ge1$. Let $z_j,\bar z_j$ be complex coordinate notation for the real and imaginary coordinates of $N$ commuting spinor-mode amplitudes. On the complexified canonical coordinate space impose
$$\{z_j,p_k\}=\delta_{jk},\qquad \{\bar z_j,\bar p_k\}=\delta_{jk},$$
with all other elementary brackets zero, extended by bilinearity and the Leibniz rule. The first-order kinetic term $\frac{i\hbar}{2}\sum_j(\bar z_j\dot z_j-\dot{\bar z}_jz_j)$ gives primary constraints
$$C_j=p_j-\frac{i\hbar}{2}\bar z_j,\qquad \bar C_j=\bar p_j+\frac{i\hbar}{2}z_j.$$
In the order $(C_1,\ldots,C_N,\bar C_1,\ldots,\bar C_N)$ their constraint matrix and inverse are
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\hbar I_N\\i\hbar I_N&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-iI_N/\hbar\\iI_N/\hbar&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Thus the constraints are second class. The Dirac bracket
$$\{F,G\}_D=\{F,G\}-\{F,\chi_A\}(M^{-1})_{AB}\{\chi_B,G\}, \quad \chi=(C_1,\ldots,C_N,\bar C_1,\ldots,\bar C_N),$$
satisfies $\{z_j,\bar z_k\}_D=-i\delta_{jk}/\hbar$ and $\{z_j,z_k\}_D=\{\bar z_j,\bar z_k\}_D=0$. For a real smooth finite-mode Hamiltonian $H(z,\bar z)$ the reduced equation is $i\hbar\dot z_j=\partial H/\partial\bar z_j$. These are ordinary commuting coordinates; they do not derive CAR by canonical quantization.

derivations.claim:
In the adopted action, $\rho_q:=q_{\rm SI}\psi^\dagger\psi$ is the
coefficient of the scalar-potential coupling. For the Dirac part, $x^0=ct$
and $A_0=-\varphi/c$ give
$D_0\psi=c^{-1}(\dot\psi+iq_{\rm SI}\varphi\psi/\hbar)$ and
$D_0\bar\psi=c^{-1}(\dot{\bar\psi}-iq_{\rm SI}\varphi\bar\psi/\hbar)$.
Using [F5], the time part of $\hbar c\mathcal L_{\rm nat}$ is the canonical
term $i\hbar(\psi^\dagger\dot\psi-\dot\psi^\dagger\psi)/2$ minus
$q_{\rm SI}\varphi\psi^\dagger\psi$. The symmetric spatial derivative,
integrated by parts on the periodic torus, is
$i\hbar c\psi^\dagger\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\nabla\psi$: the integral
of $\nabla\cdot(\psi^\dagger\boldsymbol\alpha\psi)$ vanishes because
opposite periodic faces cancel. The spatial vector-coupling term in the
Lagrangian is $q_{\rm SI}c\psi^\dagger\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf A\psi$,
and the mass term is $-m_{\rm SI}c^2\psi^\dagger\beta\psi$. The
first-order canonical momenta are $i\hbar\psi^\dagger/2$ and
$-i\hbar\psi/2$, so their pairing with the time derivatives cancels the
canonical term. Negating the remaining Dirac Lagrangian terms in the Legendre
transform gives the matter Hamiltonian density
$\psi^\dagger[c\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot(-i\hbar\nabla-q_{\rm SI}\mathbf A)
+\beta m_{\rm SI}c^2+q_{\rm SI}\varphi]\psi$, whose scalar term is
$\varphi\rho_q$. On stationary fields this source agrees with [F4].

The finite-mode calculation is separate from the field branch. For
$N\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$, [L2] gives the displayed constraint matrix
$M=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\hbar I_N\\i\hbar I_N&0\end{pmatrix}$.
Its determinant is $(-i\hbar)^{2N}\ne0$, so the primary constraints are
second class. The reduced bracket from [L2] is
$\{z_j,\bar z_k\}_D=-i\delta_{jk}/\hbar$; the calculation uses
commuting classical coordinates only and does not derive fermionic CAR.

From [F1]–[F3], $S_0^2=\mu_0\hbar c$ and
$F_{\rm SI}=S_0f$, so the physical Maxwell Lagrangian density is
$-F_{ab}^{\rm SI}F_{\rm SI}^{ab}/(4\mu_0)$. The tensor conventions [F2]
give
$F_{ab}^{\rm SI}F_{\rm SI}^{ab}=2(|\mathbf B|^2-|\mathbf E|^2/c^2)$;
using $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ from [F1], this becomes
$\mathcal L_M=\varepsilon_0|\dot{\mathbf A}+\nabla\varphi|^2/2
-|\mathbf B|^2/(2\mu_0)$. Differentiating with respect to
$\dot{\mathbf A}$ gives
$\boldsymbol\pi_A=\varepsilon_0(\dot{\mathbf A}+\nabla\varphi)
=-\varepsilon_0\mathbf E$; there is no $\dot\varphi$ term, so
$\pi_\varphi=0$. Since
$\dot{\mathbf A}=\boldsymbol\pi_A/\varepsilon_0-\nabla\varphi$,
the Maxwell Legendre transform is
$|\boldsymbol\pi_A|^2/(2\varepsilon_0)+|\mathbf B|^2/(2\mu_0)
-\boldsymbol\pi_A\cdot\nabla\varphi$. Integrating the last term by
parts on the torus gives $+\varphi\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\pi_A$;
opposite periodic faces cancel. Adding the matter Hamiltonian from step 1.1
gives exactly the Hamiltonian in the Statement, including
$\varphi(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\pi_A+\rho_q)$.

Varying the unrestricted multiplier $\varphi$ in step 2.1 imposes
$\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\pi_A+\rho_q=0$. Substituting
$\boldsymbol\pi_A=-\varepsilon_0\mathbf E$ gives
$\varepsilon_0\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\rho_q$. In Coulomb gauge,
$\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=-\Delta\varphi$ because
$\nabla\cdot\dot{\mathbf A}=0$, so the constraint becomes
$-\Delta\varphi=\rho_q/\varepsilon_0$. This is the Gauss sign in [F3].
The multiplier equation holds for every smooth periodic source; neutrality
is needed only for a periodic solution.

Under the neutral-branch hypothesis in the Statement, the smoothness,
periodicity, and zero-mean hypotheses of [L1] hold at each $t\in I$.
It supplies the unique zero-mean Fourier solution and energy identity. Each
summand is nonnegative because $\varepsilon_0>0$ by [F1] and
$|2\pi\mathbf n/L|^2>0$ for $\mathbf n\ne0$; hence the longitudinal
energy is nonnegative. This remains conditional on the current draft solver
and Countable Choice and asserts no solution for nonneutral data.

On the neutral branch [A3], [F1] and step 1.1 give
$\rho_q=-e_{\rm SI}\psi^\dagger\psi$ and
$\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\psi^\dagger\psi\,d^3\mathbf x=0$ because
$e_{\rm SI}>0$. The integrand is continuous and nonnegative. If it were
positive at any point, continuity would make it positive on a ball of
positive volume, forcing a positive integral. Thus it vanishes everywhere
and $\psi=0$. The finite-mode calculation of step 1.2 is logically
separate and does not assert a solution in this neutral branch.

facts.label: A1
facts.text:
[A1] [[post-qft-qed-local-coupling]]: the selected model adopts the smooth
local Maxwell–Dirac action. This postulate expressly does not assert its
Euler–Lagrange consequences, including the Gauss constraint.

facts.label: A2
facts.text:
[A2] Countable Choice is carried from the torus Fourier supplier used for
the neutral existence branch. [[def-countable-choice]]

facts.label: F1
facts.text:
[F1] [[pthm-qft-qed-coulomb-constraints]]: under its smooth periodic torus
hypotheses, variation of the scalar-potential multiplier in the adopted
action yields $\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A+\rho_q=0$. This is a
derived model consequence. Neutrality is additionally required for the
periodic Coulomb-potential solver, not for the multiplier equation itself.

facts.label: F2
facts.text:
[F2] [[def-qft-framework-units]]: $\psi$ has canonical length dimension
$\mathrm m^{-3/2}$, and the spatial coordinates have units metre.

facts.label: L1
facts.text:
[L1] [[lem-qft-qed-coulomb-constraint]] (draft carrier with a current escalated Step 1
decision through its QFT QED-gauge-data prerequisite): for smooth real periodic source density on the flat torus,
a smooth periodic solution of $-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ requires
zero spatial mean; when that condition holds, the unique zero-mean smooth
solution has the stated Fourier coefficients and nonnegative energy identity.
This is a conditional solver for smooth periodic data, not a quantum density
product construction.

facts.label: A3
facts.text:
[A3] Hypothetically, $L>0$, $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}<0$,
$\psi(\mathbf x)=\psi_0\ne0$ is constant, and the model has no boundary,
puncture, or compensating exterior flux.

steps.text:
By [A3], $\rho_q=q_{\rm SI}\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0$ is constant; its
SI density unit is $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$ by [F2] and the stated charge
convention. Thus $Q=q_{\rm SI}\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0L^3<0$ because
$q_{\rm SI}<0$, $\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0>0$, and $L>0$. A smooth periodic
solution of [F1] would satisfy
$\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A=-\rho_q$. Integrate this equality over
the fundamental cube $[0,L]^3$. For each coordinate $i$, the integral of
$\partial_i(\pi_A)_i$ in that coordinate is the value on the face
$x_i=L$ minus the value on $x_i=0$; these are equal by periodicity, so
each face difference is zero. Fubini for the smooth functions on the
compact cube then gives
$\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A\,d^3\mathbf x=0$.
It follows that $Q=\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\rho_q\,d^3\mathbf x=0$, contradicting
the strict inequality in this step. [A1, F1, F2, A3, algebra]
steps.claim:
By [A3], $\rho_q=q_{\rm SI}\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0$ is constant; its
SI density unit is $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$ by [F2] and the stated charge
convention. Thus $Q=q_{\rm SI}\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0L^3<0$ because
$q_{\rm SI}<0$, $\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0>0$, and $L>0$. A smooth periodic
solution of [F1] would satisfy
$\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A=-\rho_q$. Integrate this equality over

$x_i=L$ minus the value on $x_i=0$; these are equal by periodicity, so
each face difference is zero. Fubini for the smooth functions on the
compact cube then gives
$\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A\,d^3\mathbf x=0$.
It follows that $Q=\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\rho_q\,d^3\mathbf x=0$, contradicting
the strict inequality in this step.

steps.text:

citations.quote:
Adopt a smooth local classical Maxwell–Dirac model on an open region of the
flat spacetime specified by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Let $A_{{\rm SI},a}$
be a supplied real $C^\infty$ electromagnetic covector potential and let
$\psi:\!U\to\mathbb C^4$ be a $C^\infty$ commuting spinor field. The charge
$q_{\rm SI}$ and rest mass $m_{\rm SI}>0$ are model inputs; for the electron
take $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$. Use the component, metric, Clifford, charge,
field-normalization, and unit conventions of
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]], [[def-qft-qed-physical-gauge-quantities]],
[[def-qft-framework-units]], and the electromagnetic suppliers of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]]. In particular,
$D_a=\partial_a-iq_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar
=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a$ and $\mu=m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$.

Adopt the local action density in natural normalization

$$\mathcal L_{\rm nat} =-\frac14 f_{ab}f^{ab} +\frac{i}{2}\bigl(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi -(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\bigr)-\mu\bar\psi\psi,$$

where $f_{ab}=\partial_a a_b-\partial_ba_a$ on the region where the
potential is supplied, $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$, and
$D_a\bar\psi=\partial_a\bar\psi+iq_{\rm n}a_a\bar\psi$. The physical action
is $S_{\rm cl}=\hbar\int_U\mathcal L_{\rm nat}\,d^4x$ with $x^0=ct$. For
compactly supported local variations this is the adopted classical
Maxwell–Dirac formulation; its Euler–Lagrange consequences are not postulated
as a proof in this item.

For a smooth gauge function $\chi$ in webers, the adopted local
transformation is
$A_{{\rm SI},a}\mapsto A_{{\rm SI},a}+\partial_a\chi$ and
$\psi\mapsto e^{iq_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar}\psi$. It leaves $F=dA$ invariant and
makes $D_a\psi$ transform by the same phase. This is the covector form of the
SI potential rule in [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. Gauge functions in the
local variation argument are compactly supported; no assertion is made about
large gauge transformations, nontrivial bundles, boundary charges, or
asymptotic sectors.

The model adopts the separately specified free Dirac representation of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]] and the positive free photon representation of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]] as the free-field correspondence used to
describe the selected species. This extra correspondence does not quantize
the interacting classical action. In particular, this postulate supplies no
interacting continuum four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, no globally
well-posed coupled PDE, no pointwise operator-valued composite current, no
scattering or LSZ construction, and no regulator-removal or
nonperturbative-existence result.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] for the torus Fourier
construction. Let $L>0$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time
interval, and let the spatial domain be the flat torus
$\mathbb T_L^3=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$, where $L$ is a positive length
in metres. Coordinates use $x^0=ct$ with $t$ in seconds under
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. Use the smooth classical branch of
[[post-qft-qed-local-coupling]] with smooth periodic electromagnetic
potentials and spinor. Here $\psi$ has the canonical length dimension
$\mathrm m^{-3/2}$ of [[def-qft-framework-units]], so the scalar-potential
source $\rho_q:=q_{\rm SI}\psi^\dagger\psi$ has unit $\mathrm{C,m^{-3}}$.
On stationary solutions it agrees
with the current density in [[pthm-qft-qed-classical-coupling]]. Use the
gamma-matrix and
$\alpha,\beta$ conventions of [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. In Coulomb gauge
$\operatorname{div}\mathbf A=0$, the multiplier equation for any smooth
periodic configuration is
$\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A+\rho_q=0$. On the explicitly neutral
branch
$\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\rho_q(\mathbf x,t)\,d^3\mathbf x=0$ for every $t\in I$,
the zero-mean scalar potential is the unique smooth periodic solution of
$-\Delta\varphi=\rho_q/\varepsilon_0$. With
$\widehat\rho_q(\mathbf n,t)=L^{-3}\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}
\rho_q(\mathbf x,t)e^{-2\pi i\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf x/L}\,d^3\mathbf x$ and
$\boldsymbol\kappa_{\mathbf n}=2\pi\mathbf n/L$, the longitudinal energy is

$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}|\nabla\varphi|^2\,d^3\mathbf x =\frac12\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\rho_q\varphi\,d^3\mathbf x =\frac{L^3}{2\varepsilon_0} \sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}} \frac{|\widehat\rho_q(\mathbf n,t)|^2}{|\boldsymbol\kappa_{\mathbf n}|^2} \ge0.$$

The corresponding classical Hamiltonian, before imposing the Gauss
constraint, contains

$$H=\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\left[ \frac{|\boldsymbol\pi_A|^2}{2\varepsilon_0} +\frac{|\mathbf B|^2}{2\mu_0} +\psi^\dagger\!\left(c\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot (-i\hbar\nabla-q_{\rm SI}\mathbf A)+\beta m_{\rm SI}c^2\right)\!\psi +\varphi(\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A+\rho_q) \right]d^3\mathbf x,$$

with $\pi_\varphi=0$ the primary multiplier momentum. In a separate
truncation to $N\ge1$ orthonormal spatial spinor modes, let $z_j,\bar z_j$
be dimensionless commuting complex-coordinate notation with canonical
brackets $\{z_j,p_k\}=\delta_{jk}$,
$\{\bar z_j,\bar p_k\}=\delta_{jk}$ and all other elementary brackets zero.
For $\hbar>0$, the symmetrized first-order Dirac kinetic term gives the
primary constraints
$C_j=p_j-i\hbar\bar z_j/2$ and
$\bar C_j=\bar p_j+i\hbar z_j/2$ with invertible mixed bracket matrix
$-i\hbar I_N$. This finite-dimensional classical calculation does not
derive fermionic CAR. The neutral torus branch is an explicit hypothesis.
For the selected electron, $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}\ne0$, so a neutral
single-species commuting-spinor configuration has $\psi=0$; no nontrivial
neutral charged classical Dirac configuration is asserted. The finite-mode
constraint calculation is separate and does not claim to be a solution in
that branch.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For spatial wave vector $\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ put
$\omega(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here
$\omega$ is the temporal wave number, not the SI angular frequency; the
corresponding SI angular frequency is $c\omega$. Energy and momentum are
$E=\hbar c\omega$ in joules and $\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in
$\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$ the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

The natural action is $S/\hbar$. Its canonical density in four dimensions has
unit $\mathrm m^{-4}$; the corresponding physical energy density is
$\hbar c$ times that density and has unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
write $\phi_{\rm n}$ for a scalar field with length degree $-1$ and
$\psi_{\rm n}$ for a Dirac field with length degree $-3/2$. These are the
dimensions fixed by the selected free kinetic terms, not exact scaling
dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous dimensions, when present, are
separate quantities. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

The Clifford convention is $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$,
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}$, so the effective Clifford metric is
$-\eta$. In a supplied free Dirac model the displayed equation is
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$. The phase and Clifford choices are
conventions; this item proves no Dirac representation or field equation.
Time evolution is written $U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$ when a selected model has
actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ and its unitary group; the
corresponding Heisenberg conjugation is $O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. No such
Hamiltonian or group is constructed here. Where a free-field module uses an
inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the repository's
first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction.
Smeared fields are not thereby bounded, symmetric, self-adjoint, or
self-adjointly closable. Locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior are likewise supplied only by the
relevant constructed model modules. Test-function units can be chosen so a
specified smeared observable is dimensionless; there is no universal test
function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

Assume Countable Choice and the conventions of [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. On the periodic box $T_L^3=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$, take smooth real periodic charge and current densities $ho,\mathbf J$, smooth periodic $\mathbf A,\dot{\mathbf A},\phi$, and $L,\epsilon_0,\mu_0>0$. Define the formal classical density
$$\mathcal L= rac{\epsilon_0}{2}|\dot{\mathbf A}+
abla\phi|^2- rac1{2\mu_0}|
abla	imes\mathbf A|^2-ho\phi+\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf A.$$
The canonical momenta are $ oldsymbol\pi_A=\epsilon_0(\dot{\mathbf A}+
abla\phi)$ and $\pi_\phi=0$. Periodic integration by parts gives
$$H=\int_{T_L^3}\left( rac{| oldsymbol\pi_A|^2}{2\epsilon_0}+ rac{|
abla	imes\mathbf A|^2}{2\mu_0} +\phi(
abla\cdot oldsymbol\pi_A+ho)-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf Aight)d^3x.$$
Variation of the multiplier $\phi$ imposes $
abla\cdot oldsymbol\pi_A+ho=0$. In Coulomb gauge $
abla\cdot\mathbf A=0$, this becomes $-\Delta\phi=ho/\epsilon_0$. Such a smooth periodic solution exists only if $\int_{T_L^3}ho\,d^3x=0$. If this neutrality condition holds, there is a unique zero-mean solution, with Fourier coefficients
$$\widehat\phi_0=0,\qquad \widehat\phi_k= rac{\widehatho_k}{\epsilon_0|2\pi k/L|^2}\quad(k
e0),\qquad \widehatho_k=L^{-3}\int_{[0,L]^3}ho(x)e^{-2\pi i k\cdot x/L}\,d^3x.$$
It is smooth and satisfies
$$ rac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int|
abla\phi|^2\,d^3x = rac12\intho\phi\,d^3x = rac{L^3}{2\epsilon_0}\sum_{k
e0} rac{|\widehatho_k|^2}{|2\pi k/L|^2}\ge0.$$
This is a classical conditional solver for smooth periodic neutral data; it makes no claim about quantum density products or nonperiodic boundary conditions.

derivations.claim:
By [A3], $\rho_q=q_{\rm SI}\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0$ is constant; its
SI density unit is $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$ by [F2] and the stated charge
convention. Thus $Q=q_{\rm SI}\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0L^3<0$ because
$q_{\rm SI}<0$, $\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0>0$, and $L>0$. A smooth periodic
solution of [F1] would satisfy
$\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A=-\rho_q$. Integrate this equality over
the fundamental cube $[0,L]^3$. For each coordinate $i$, the integral of
$\partial_i(\pi_A)_i$ in that coordinate is the value on the face
$x_i=L$ minus the value on $x_i=0$; these are equal by periodicity, so
each face difference is zero. Fubini for the smooth functions on the
compact cube then gives
$\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A\,d^3\mathbf x=0$.
It follows that $Q=\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\rho_q\,d^3\mathbf x=0$, contradicting
the strict inequality in this step.

Independently, [L1] records the same compatibility requirement for
the Coulomb equation: a smooth periodic potential can exist only for
zero-mean charge density. Thus the contradiction is a consequence of the
specified periodic model and boundary conditions; adding a boundary,
puncture, or compensating source changes the hypotheses and is not
covered.

facts.label: F1
facts.text:
[F1] [[post-qft-qed-local-coupling]]: the adopted natural action is
$$ \mathcal L_{\rm nat}=-\frac14 f_{ab}f^{ab} +\frac i2(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi-(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi) -\mu\bar\psi\psi, $$
with $D_a=\partial_a-iq_n a_a$, $x^0=ct$, $\mu=mc/\hbar$, and
compactly supported local variations. Its own text leaves the
Euler–Lagrange consequence for a consuming proof.

facts.label: F2
facts.text:

[[def-qft-qed-physical-gauge-quantities]]: $\eta=(-,+,+,+)$,
$A_0=-\phi/c$, $a_a=A_a/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$, and
$q_na_a=q_{\rm SI}A_a/\hbar$; $\gamma^0=\beta$,
$\gamma^i=\beta\alpha_i$, $\beta^2=I_4$, and
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

facts.label: F3
facts.text:

$\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$, real $q$, $m>0$, and the common core
$\mathcal D$, it proves $[\pi_i,\pi_j]=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ and the
displayed square identity; it derives the formal $K/(2m)$ coefficient and
its spin term without assuming self-adjointness.

facts.label: F4
facts.text:

$\beta=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,-I_2)$,
$\alpha_i=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_i\\\sigma_i&0\end{pmatrix}$,

$\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$. Its current Step 1 record is escalated:
the QFT-MF01 page review remains open and the active run records the
QFT-MF02 artifact as missing. The present calculation uses only the explicit

facts.label: A1
facts.text:
[A1] [[post-qft-qed-local-coupling]] is an adopted classical local model
with commuting smooth spinor variables. Its physical interpretation does
not quantize the interacting action or supply a continuum QED solution.

steps.text: Let $\chi$ be a compactly supported smooth complex spinor variation and write $\delta\bar\psi=\bar\chi$. Vary the symmetrized spinor action in [F1] while holding $a_a$ fixed. Since $\gamma^a$ is constant and $D_a\bar\chi=\partial_a\bar\chi+iq_na_a\bar\chi$, compact integration by parts gives $\int(D_a\bar\chi)\gamma^a\psi\,d^4x=-\int\bar\chi\gamma^aD_a\psi\,d^4x$: the derivative term changes sign, and the connection term becomes $+iq_na_a$ on the right, matching the conjugate-charge term on the left. Thus $\delta(S_{\rm cl}/\hbar)=2\operatorname{Re}\int\chi^\dagger\beta(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi\,d^4x$. No field product outside the smooth classical action is used. [given, F1, F2, A1, algebra]
steps.claim: Let $\chi$ be a compactly supported smooth complex spinor variation and write $\delta\bar\psi=\bar\chi$. Vary the symmetrized spinor action in [F1] while holding $a_a$ fixed. Since $\gamma^a$ is constant and $D_a\bar\chi=\partial_a\bar\chi+iq_na_a\bar\chi$, compact integration by parts gives $\int(D_a\bar\chi)\gamma^a\psi\,d^4x=-\int\bar\chi\gamma^aD_a\psi\,d^4x$: the derivative term changes sign, and the connection term becomes $+iq_na_a$ on the right, matching the conjugate-charge term on the left. Thus $\delta(S_{\rm cl}/\hbar)=2\operatorname{Re}\int\chi^\dagger\beta(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi\,d^4x$. No field product outside the smooth classical action is used.

steps.text: Put $R=(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi$. If the first variation vanishes for all compactly supported $\chi$, choose $\chi=\rho\beta R$ for any nonnegative compactly supported smooth real bump $\rho$. Since $\beta^2=I$ and $\beta=\beta^\dagger$, this gives $0=2\int\rho\,R^\dagger R\,d^4x$. If $R$ were nonzero at a point, continuity would make $R^\dagger R>0$ on a neighborhood, and a bump supported there would make the integral positive; hence $R=0$ pointwise. Conversely, if $R=0$, the first variation in 1.1 vanishes. Therefore the compact spinor-variation Euler–Lagrange equation is $(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi=0$. [given, step 1.1, F2, algebra]
steps.claim: Put $R=(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi$. If the first variation vanishes for all compactly supported $\chi$, choose $\chi=\rho\beta R$ for any nonnegative compactly supported smooth real bump $\rho$. Since $\beta^2=I$ and $\beta=\beta^\dagger$, this gives $0=2\int\rho\,R^\dagger R\,d^4x$. If $R$ were nonzero at a point, continuity would make $R^\dagger R>0$ on a neighborhood, and a bump supported there would make the integral positive; hence $R=0$ pointwise. Conversely, if $R=0$, the first variation in 1.1 vanishes. Therefore the compact spinor-variation Euler–Lagrange equation is $(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi=0$.

steps.text: With $A_0=0$, the conversion in [F2] gives $$ D_0=c^{-1}\partial_t,\qquad D_i=\partial_i-iqA_i/\hbar. $$ Use $\gamma^0=\beta$ and $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha_i$ in the Euler–Lagrange equation just obtained, multiply on the left by $\beta$, and use $\mu=mc/\hbar$. After multiplication by $\hbar c$, the result is $$ i\hbar\partial_t\psi= [c\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot(-i\hbar\boldsymbol\nabla-q\mathbf A) +\beta mc^2]\psi=H_D\psi. $$ This is an equality of the stated differential expressions. It establishes the QX12 Hamiltonian convention on $\mathcal D$ and assumes no operator closure. [given, step 2.1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]
steps.claim: With $A_0=0$, the conversion in [F2] gives $$ D_0=c^{-1}\partial_t,\qquad D_i=\partial_i-iqA_i/\hbar. $$ Use $\gamma^0=\beta$ and $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha_i$ in the Euler–Lagrange equation just obtained, multiply on the left by $\beta$, and use $\mu=mc/\hbar$. After multiplication by $\hbar c$, the result is $$ i\hbar\partial_t\psi= [c\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot(-i\hbar\boldsymbol\nabla-q\mathbf A) +\beta mc^2]\psi=H_D\psi. $$ This is an equality of the stated differential expressions. It establishes the QX12 Hamiltonian convention on $\mathcal D$ and assumes no operator closure.

steps.text: The smooth multiplication and derivative maps preserve $\mathcal D$. By [F3], their commutator is $[\pi_i,\pi_j]=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ there, and the Pauli-block identity $\alpha_i\alpha_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k$ contracts the antisymmetric part to $$ \frac i2\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k[\pi_i,\pi_j] =-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B. $$ The cross terms with $\beta mc^2$ cancel because $\alpha_i\beta+\beta\alpha_i=0$, while $\beta^2=I$. Hence the exact core identity in the Statement follows, with every product acting on $\mathcal D$. [given, step 3.1, F3, F4, algebra]
steps.claim: The smooth multiplication and derivative maps preserve $\mathcal D$. By [F3], their commutator is $[\pi_i,\pi_j]=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ there, and the Pauli-block identity $\alpha_i\alpha_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k$ contracts the antisymmetric part to $$ \frac i2\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k[\pi_i,\pi_j] =-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B. $$ The cross terms with $\beta mc^2$ cancel because $\alpha_i\beta+\beta\alpha_i=0$, while $\beta^2=I$. Hence the exact core identity in the Statement follows, with every product acting on $\mathcal D$.

steps.text: In a formal symbol $t$, square $mc^2+t aK+O(t^2)$ and equate it to $m^2c^4+t c^2K+O(t^2)$. The coefficient of $t$ gives $2mc^2aK=c^2K$, so $a=1/(2m)$ since $m>0$. The spin part of $K/(2m)$ is $$ -\frac{q\hbar}{2m}\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B =-\frac qm\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B. $$ Equating this with $-g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$ and using $q=-e\ne0$ and the nonzero Pauli spin matrices gives $g_s=2$. This is a formal coefficient comparison only, not a source-reported empirical estimate under the type distinction [F6]. [given, step 4.1, F3, F6, algebra] ∎
steps.claim: In a formal symbol $t$, square $mc^2+t aK+O(t^2)$ and equate it to $m^2c^4+t c^2K+O(t^2)$. The coefficient of $t$ gives $2mc^2aK=c^2K$, so $a=1/(2m)$ since $m>0$. The spin part of $K/(2m)$ is $$ -\frac{q\hbar}{2m}\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B =-\frac qm\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B. $$ Equating this with $-g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$ and using $q=-e\ne0$ and the nonzero Pauli spin matrices gives $g_s=2$. This is a formal coefficient comparison only, not a source-reported empirical estimate under the type distinction [F6].

citations.quote:
Adopt a smooth local classical Maxwell–Dirac model on an open region of the
flat spacetime specified by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Let $A_{{\rm SI},a}$
be a supplied real $C^\infty$ electromagnetic covector potential and let
$\psi:\!U\to\mathbb C^4$ be a $C^\infty$ commuting spinor field. The charge
$q_{\rm SI}$ and rest mass $m_{\rm SI}>0$ are model inputs; for the electron
take $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$. Use the component, metric, Clifford, charge,
field-normalization, and unit conventions of
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]], [[def-qft-qed-physical-gauge-quantities]],
[[def-qft-framework-units]], and the electromagnetic suppliers of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]]. In particular,
$D_a=\partial_a-iq_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar
=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a$ and $\mu=m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$.

Adopt the local action density in natural normalization

$$\mathcal L_{\rm nat}
=-\frac14 f_{ab}f^{ab}
+\frac{i}{2}\bigl(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi
-(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\bigr)-\mu\bar\psi\psi,$$

where $f_{ab}=\partial_a a_b-\partial_ba_a$ on the region where the
potential is supplied, $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$, and
$D_a\bar\psi=\partial_a\bar\psi+iq_{\rm n}a_a\bar\psi$. The physical action
is $S_{\rm cl}=\hbar\int_U\mathcal L_{\rm nat}\,d^4x$ with $x^0=ct$. For
compactly supported local variations this is the adopted classical
Maxwell–Dirac formulation; its Euler–Lagrange consequences are not postulated
as a proof in this item.

For a smooth gauge function $\chi$ in webers, the adopted local
transformation is
$A_{{\rm SI},a}\mapsto A_{{\rm SI},a}+\partial_a\chi$ and
$\psi\mapsto e^{iq_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar}\psi$. It leaves $F=dA$ invariant and
makes $D_a\psi$ transform by the same phase. This is the covector form of the
SI potential rule in [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. Gauge functions in the
local variation argument are compactly supported; no assertion is made about
large gauge transformations, nontrivial bundles, boundary charges, or
asymptotic sectors.

The model adopts the separately specified free Dirac representation of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]] and the positive free photon representation of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]] as the free-field correspondence used to
describe the selected species. This extra correspondence does not quantize
the interacting classical action. In particular, this postulate supplies no
interacting continuum four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, no globally
well-posed coupled PDE, no pointwise operator-valued composite current, no
scattering or LSZ construction, and no regulator-removal or
nonperturbative-existence result.

Use smooth fields on Minkowski coordinate space with $x^0=ct$ and $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Components of $x$ are measured in metres. Fix the Dirac matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], so $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ and $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$.

For the SI-normalization bookkeeping, let $c>0$ (m s$^{-1}$), $\hbar>0$ (J s), $\mu_0>0$ (N A$^{-2}$), a real charge parameter $q$ (C), and a mass parameter $m>0$ (kg) be symbolic inputs; put $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. In the current SI, $c$ and $h$ are defining constants while $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined; the formula below keeps $\mu_0$ symbolic and assigns it no numerical value. Use the lower-potential convention
$$A_a=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A),\qquad F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a,$$
where $A_a$ has units T m, $\phi$ is in volts, and $\mathbf A$ is in T m. Define
$$S_0=\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c},\qquad a_a=A_a/S_0,\qquad f_{ab}=\partial_aa_b-\partial_ba_a,$$
$$\mu=mc/\hbar,\qquad g=q\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}=q/\sqrt{\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad D_a=\partial_a-ig a_a.$$
Thus $a_a$ and $\mu$ have units m$^{-1}$, $f_{ab}$ has units m$^{-2}$, and $g$ is dimensionless. For $\psi$ with units m$^{-3/2}$, both $-\tfrac14 f_{ab}f^{ab}$ and $\bar\psi(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi$ have units m$^{-4}$; their integral over $d^4x$ is dimensionless and represents the action divided by $\hbar$ in this normalization.

For a real smooth gauge parameter $\chi$ in webers, put $\alpha=\chi/S_0$ (dimensionless) and use
$$A'_a=A_a+\partial_a\chi,\qquad a'_a=a_a+\partial_a\alpha,\qquad \psi'=e^{ig\alpha}\psi.$$
The induced covariant derivative is $D'_a=\partial_a-ig a'_a$. These are formal mathematical conventions for the later conditional deductions. They do not adopt a measured value of $\mu_0$, identify $q$ with an electron charge, impose charge quantization, or assert that interacting continuum fields exist.

Use the oriented, time-oriented Minkowski model, length coordinates, metric,
and SI/natural dictionary of [[def-qft-framework-units]], with
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $x^0=ct$. Use the gamma matrices,
Dirac adjoint, and effective Clifford metric of
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]: $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$,
and $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$. Assume Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]] for the mathematical QFT gauge-data supplier; the
unit conversions below do not themselves spend a choice principle.

Identify the SI charge and mass symbols $q,m$ in
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]] with $q_{\rm SI},m_{\rm SI}$ here. Its natural
coupling $g$ is $q_{\rm n}$ below, and its inverse-length mass $\mu$ is the
same $m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$.

Let $q_{\rm SI}\in\mathbb R$ be a selected charge parameter in coulombs and
$m_{\rm SI}>0$ a selected rest-mass parameter in kilograms. They are inputs
of the chosen model; neither is derived from Maxwell's equations. Set
$\mu=m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and
$q_{\rm n}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$, which is dimensionless under the
framework units of [[def-qft-framework-units]]. For an electron use
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ and
$e_{\rm n}=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}>0$, so $q_{\rm n}=-e_{\rm n}$.
Use $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the measured current-SI
$\mu_0$ of [[def-qft-framework-units]]. These definitions therefore do not
assign an exact numerical value to $q_{\rm n}$, $e_{\rm n}$, or
$\varepsilon_0$.

In a named inertial chart, let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ be the
electromagnetic potential when one is supplied, with components in
$\mathrm{T\,m}$ under [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]. Define the canonical potential and
field-strength components by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have engineering dimensions $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\mathrm m^{-2}$,
respectively. With the metric-lowered potential
$A_{{\rm SI},a}=\eta_{ab}A^b_{\rm SI}$, the potential component convention is
$A_{{\rm SI},0}=-\varphi/c$ and $A_{{\rm SI},i}=A_i$. The covariant derivative
in the selected QED model is

$$D_a:=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a =\partial_a-\frac{iq_{\rm SI}}{\hbar}A_{{\rm SI},a},$$

since $q_{\rm n}a_a=q_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar$. Both terms in $D_a$
have unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. If the SI gauge function $\chi$ has unit
$\mathrm{Wb}=\mathrm{T\,m^2}$, then $q_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar$ is dimensionless;
the corresponding natural gauge function
$\lambda=\chi/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ is dimensionless and
$q_{\rm n}\lambda=q_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar$. These conversions apply to smooth
local gauge transformations; they assert no boundary condition, asymptotic
charge sector, or global gauge-fixing result.

If a separately specified finite regulator introduces Hamiltonian
eigenvalues, they have unit joule; this definition introduces no regulator.
The field components and units refer to the selected inertial chart, not to a
new observer congruence or a cross-framework identification.

Let $m>0$ be a particle mass in kilograms, $q\in\mathbb R$ its charge in coulombs, and $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ a smooth spatial vector potential with components in tesla-metres. Set $B_k=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iA_j$ and define on the common core $\mathcal C=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$
$$\pi_i=-i\hbar\partial_i-qA_i,\qquad H_D=c\sum_i\alpha_i\pi_i+\beta mc^2,\qquad \Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i,\sigma_i).$$
Here the matrices are those of [[lem-qft-example-spin-trace-completeness]] and $\hbar,c$ have the SI conventions of [[def-qft-example-data]]. These differential maps preserve $\mathcal C$, and on $\mathcal C$,
$$[\pi_i,\pi_j]=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k,\qquad H_D^2=m^2c^4I_4+c^2(\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B).$$
If the formal first-order square-root coefficient is written as $mc^2+K/(2m)$ with $K=\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B$, then its spin term is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$, where $\mathbf S=\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma/2$. Under the coefficient convention $H_{\mathrm{mag}}=-\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}\cdot\mathbf B$ and $\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}=g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S$, equality of the formal coefficients as a linear function of $q$ gives $g_s=2$ for the minimal tree-level term. No magnetic self-adjoint closure, full spectrum, operator square-root theorem, radiative correction, or empirical prediction is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical scalar shell conventions of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and the second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Let $\mathcal H_D$ be the space of measurable functions $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^4$, modulo equality almost everywhere, with
$$\|u\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(\mathbf k)^\dagger u(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}<\infty,$$
and pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u(\mathbf k)^\dagger v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$. Define the measurable matrix $h_D(\mathbf k)=\sum_j\alpha_j k_j+\beta\mu$ and its maximal multiplication operator with domain $D(h_D)=\{u\in\mathcal H_D:h_Du\in\mathcal H_D\}$. For $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix fields
$$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=\frac12\left(I_4\pm\frac{h_D(\mathbf k)}{\omega(\mathbf k)}\right).$$
When $\mu=0$ at $\mathbf k=0$, set $P_+(0)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,0)$ and $P_-(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,I_2)$. These are complementary rank-two orthogonal projections; the value at this Lebesgue-null point does not change their multiplication operators. Write $M_{P_\pm}$ for their maximal multiplication operators and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}M_{P_\pm}$. The companion matrix lemma on this page proves these are bounded orthogonal projections with closed ranges. The conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ has vectors $\bar u$, scalar multiplication $z\bar u=\overline{\bar z u}$, and pairing $\langle\bar u,\bar v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$.

Use the sine and cosine definitions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. For a length-coordinate increment $t\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix multiplier
$$W_D(t,\mathbf k)=\cos(\omega t)I_4+i\frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega}h_D(\mathbf k).$$
At the massless apex set $W_D(t,0)=I_4$. Its unitarity, group law and generator identity are proved by the companion matrix lemma on this page.

The symbols $P_+$ and $P_-$ designate the positive- and negative-energy matrix formulas for this fixed free Dirac operator. This is purely mathematical data; no physical spin-statistics postulate or empirical assertion is included.

These are conventions for constructed and formal calculations in this page pair. They are not empirical claims, physical postulates, or existence claims about an interacting continuum theory.

Use the geometric spacetime metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the time coordinate $x^0=ct$ in metres. For Clifford algebra and momentum contraction use the separate algebraic metric $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$; a slash or a square of an energy four-vector uses $h$, never $\eta$.

A physical energy four-vector is $p=(E,c\mathbf p_{\rm phys})$, with each component in joules. Write $M=mc^2$ for rest energy in joules and $p^2=h(p,p)=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p_{\rm phys}|^2$. For two such vectors, $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is in $\mathrm J^2$. Natural momentum coordinates are the energy-vector components divided by $\hbar c$, in $\mathrm m^{-1}$; they are not substituted into SI formulas without restoring this factor. In the common natural-unit field convention, $\mu=mc/\hbar$ is in $\mathrm m^{-1}$, a scalar field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and a Dirac field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$.

Take SI $e>0$ in coulombs, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $c>0$ in metres per second, and $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. Define
$$\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}>0.$$
Here $g$ is a dimensionless coupling. It is not the metric and not a gyromagnetic factor.

For gauge notation set $A_{\rm lower}=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A)$, with $A_a$ in tesla-metres and gauge function $\chi$ in webers. With charge $q$ in coulombs define
$$D_a=\partial_a-\frac{iqA_a}{\hbar},\qquad \psi\mapsto e^{iq\chi/\hbar}\psi,\qquad A\mapsto A+d\chi.$$
For the electron parameter use $q=-e$. The equivalent natural-unit coordinates are $A_{\rm nat}=A_{\rm SI}/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ and $q_{\rm nat}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$.

Finite-matrix examples act on $\mathbb C^d$ with the operator norm. For Hilbert spaces, use the first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=v^\dagger u$; a displayed coordinate contraction $u^\dagger v$ is second-variable-linear and equals $\overline{(u,v)_1}$. Thus norms, traces, and modulus-squared amplitudes agree under conversion, although the unsquared pairing is conjugated. No amplitude is assigned a probability by these conventions.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For spatial wave vector $\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ put
$\omega(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here
$\omega$ is the temporal wave number, not the SI angular frequency; the
corresponding SI angular frequency is $c\omega$. Energy and momentum are
$E=\hbar c\omega$ in joules and $\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in
$\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$ the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

The natural action is $S/\hbar$. Its canonical density in four dimensions has
unit $\mathrm m^{-4}$; the corresponding physical energy density is
$\hbar c$ times that density and has unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
write $\phi_{\rm n}$ for a scalar field with length degree $-1$ and
$\psi_{\rm n}$ for a Dirac field with length degree $-3/2$. These are the
dimensions fixed by the selected free kinetic terms, not exact scaling
dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous dimensions, when present, are
separate quantities. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

The Clifford convention is $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$,
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}$, so the effective Clifford metric is
$-\eta$. In a supplied free Dirac model the displayed equation is
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$. The phase and Clifford choices are
conventions; this item proves no Dirac representation or field equation.
Time evolution is written $U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$ when a selected model has
actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ and its unitary group; the
corresponding Heisenberg conjugation is $O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. No such
Hamiltonian or group is constructed here. Where a free-field module uses an
inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the repository's
first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction.
Smeared fields are not thereby bounded, symmetric, self-adjoint, or
self-adjointly closable. Locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior are likewise supplied only by the
relevant constructed model modules. Test-function units can be chosen so a
specified smeared observable is dimensionless; there is no universal test
function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

Use the framework-local unit and domain dictionary of
[[def-qft-framework-units]] and the energy, SI/natural-unit, and finite-matrix
conventions of [[def-qft-example-data]]. A physical quantity is always typed
relative to the selected QFT formulation and its declared model data; its name
or units alone do not identify it with a quantity in another formulation.

For the **exact finite-regulator class** used on this page, the state space is
the finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$ for an integer
$d\ge1$. Model inputs include the selected Hermitian Hamiltonian matrices,
their time-dependent Hermitian interaction when present, a dimensionless
coupling parameter, an initial state, and an explicitly supplied finite
outcome measurement. A pure initial state is a vector $\psi\in\mathbb C^d$
with $\|\psi\|=1$; a mixed state is a matrix $\rho=\rho^*$ with
$\langle\rho v,v\rangle\ge0$ for every $v$ and $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$.
An exact regulated observable on this finite space is a specified Hermitian
matrix $O=O^*$ with a declared physical unit. The matrix and state are model
data; the measurement procedure and any physical rule assigning outcomes are
additional data. This definition does not say that an operator symbol by
itself is a detector outcome or probability.

A **finite probability law** on the declared outcome set
$\{1,\ldots,m\}$, $m\ge1$, is a vector $(p_1,\ldots,p_m)$ with
$p_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a=1}^m p_a=1$. It is a mathematical type. Assigning that
law to a particular preparation and measurement is a separate physical
postulate. A prediction derived from an actually constructed regulated model
is conditional on those inputs and the adopted rule.

A **formal coefficient record** is a sequence $(c_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of
specified coefficients, sometimes displayed as the symbol
$\sum_{n\ge0}c_n\lambda^n$. Unless convergence and an evaluation map are
separately proved and adopted, the symbol records coefficients only: it is not
an evaluated function, exact probability, convergent perturbation series, or
error bound. A formal coefficient can be assigned a phenomenological meaning
only by a separate, model-specific physical adoption with its approximation
scope stated.

An **empirical estimate** is a source-reported number obtained by analyzing a
finite record of measurement outcomes under the stated preparation, apparatus,
calibration, sampling, and analysis conditions. Its reported uncertainty and
conditions travel with the estimate. It is not the exact model value, and it
does not prove the framework used to interpret it. The 2022 Fan et al. report
is an example of a source-reported electron magnetic-moment determination;
this definition supplies no numerical result, uncertainty reconstruction, or
new experimental claim.

Primitive and derived status is formulation-relative. In a selected regulated
model, the regulator, Hamiltonian data, coupling, initial state, and supplied
measurement are declared inputs; an evolution, amplitude, or probability law
is derived only when the construction and adopted rule establish it. In a
formal calculation, the specified masses, couplings, coefficient rules, and
subtraction prescription are inputs, while its listed coefficients are
derived within that formal calculation. An empirical estimate is a reported
data-analysis result, not a primitive model parameter or a theorem.

The following units are examples of types, not identifications of quantities:
a cross section $\sigma$ is area-valued with SI unit $\mathrm{m^2}$; a rate
$\Gamma$ is inverse-time-valued with unit $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$; an energy width
$\Gamma_E$ has unit joule. Only a separately stated convention may identify
$\Gamma_E=\hbar\Gamma$. The fine-structure parameter $\alpha$, a dimensionless
coupling $g$, and a gyromagnetic factor $g_s$ are dimensionless but have
different physical meanings. The name “width,” a common symbol, or matching
dimensions does not supply an exponential-decay law or an equality between
these parameters.

Adopt a smooth local classical Maxwell–Dirac model on an open region of the
flat spacetime specified by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Let $A_{{\rm SI},a}$
be a supplied real $C^\infty$ electromagnetic covector potential and let
$\psi:\!U\to\mathbb C^4$ be a $C^\infty$ commuting spinor field. The charge
$q_{\rm SI}$ and rest mass $m_{\rm SI}>0$ are model inputs; for the electron
take $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$. Use the component, metric, Clifford, charge,
field-normalization, and unit conventions of
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]], [[def-qft-qed-physical-gauge-quantities]],
[[def-qft-framework-units]], and the electromagnetic suppliers of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]]. In particular,
$D_a=\partial_a-iq_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar
=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a$ and $\mu=m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$.

Adopt the local action density in natural normalization

$$\mathcal L_{\rm nat}
=-\frac14 f_{ab}f^{ab}
+\frac{i}{2}\bigl(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi
-(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\bigr)-\mu\bar\psi\psi,$$

where $f_{ab}=\partial_a a_b-\partial_ba_a$ on the region where the
potential is supplied, $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$, and
$D_a\bar\psi=\partial_a\bar\psi+iq_{\rm n}a_a\bar\psi$. The physical action
is $S_{\rm cl}=\hbar\int_U\mathcal L_{\rm nat}\,d^4x$ with $x^0=ct$. For
compactly supported local variations this is the adopted classical
Maxwell–Dirac formulation; its Euler–Lagrange consequences are not postulated
as a proof in this item.

For a smooth gauge function $\chi$ in webers, the adopted local
transformation is
$A_{{\rm SI},a}\mapsto A_{{\rm SI},a}+\partial_a\chi$ and
$\psi\mapsto e^{iq_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar}\psi$. It leaves $F=dA$ invariant and
makes $D_a\psi$ transform by the same phase. This is the covector form of the
SI potential rule in [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. Gauge functions in the
local variation argument are compactly supported; no assertion is made about
large gauge transformations, nontrivial bundles, boundary charges, or
asymptotic sectors.

The model adopts the separately specified free Dirac representation of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]] and the positive free photon representation of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]] as the free-field correspondence used to
describe the selected species. This extra correspondence does not quantize
the interacting classical action. In particular, this postulate supplies no
interacting continuum four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, no globally
well-posed coupled PDE, no pointwise operator-valued composite current, no
scattering or LSZ construction, and no regulator-removal or
nonperturbative-existence result.

Use smooth fields on Minkowski coordinate space with $x^0=ct$ and $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Components of $x$ are measured in metres. Fix the Dirac matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], so $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ and $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$.

For the SI-normalization bookkeeping, let $c>0$ (m s$^{-1}$), $\hbar>0$ (J s), $\mu_0>0$ (N A$^{-2}$), a real charge parameter $q$ (C), and a mass parameter $m>0$ (kg) be symbolic inputs; put $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. In the current SI, $c$ and $h$ are defining constants while $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined; the formula below keeps $\mu_0$ symbolic and assigns it no numerical value. Use the lower-potential convention
$$A_a=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A),\qquad F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a,$$
where $A_a$ has units T m, $\phi$ is in volts, and $\mathbf A$ is in T m. Define
$$S_0=\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c},\qquad a_a=A_a/S_0,\qquad f_{ab}=\partial_aa_b-\partial_ba_a,$$
$$\mu=mc/\hbar,\qquad g=q\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}=q/\sqrt{\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad D_a=\partial_a-ig a_a.$$
Thus $a_a$ and $\mu$ have units m$^{-1}$, $f_{ab}$ has units m$^{-2}$, and $g$ is dimensionless. For $\psi$ with units m$^{-3/2}$, both $-\tfrac14 f_{ab}f^{ab}$ and $\bar\psi(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi$ have units m$^{-4}$; their integral over $d^4x$ is dimensionless and represents the action divided by $\hbar$ in this normalization.

For a real smooth gauge parameter $\chi$ in webers, put $\alpha=\chi/S_0$ (dimensionless) and use
$$A'_a=A_a+\partial_a\chi,\qquad a'_a=a_a+\partial_a\alpha,\qquad \psi'=e^{ig\alpha}\psi.$$
The induced covariant derivative is $D'_a=\partial_a-ig a'_a$. These are formal mathematical conventions for the later conditional deductions. They do not adopt a measured value of $\mu_0$, identify $q$ with an electron charge, impose charge quantization, or assert that interacting continuum fields exist.

In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Let $\mathcal H_D$ be the space of measurable functions $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^4$, modulo equality almost everywhere, with
$$\|u\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(\mathbf k)^\dagger u(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}<\infty,$$
and pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u(\mathbf k)^\dagger v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$. Define the measurable matrix $h_D(\mathbf k)=\sum_j\alpha_j k_j+\beta\mu$ and its maximal multiplication operator with domain $D(h_D)=\{u\in\mathcal H_D:h_Du\in\mathcal H_D\}$. For $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix fields
$$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=\frac12\left(I_4\pm\frac{h_D(\mathbf k)}{\omega(\mathbf k)}\right).$$
When $\mu=0$ at $\mathbf k=0$, set $P_+(0)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,0)$ and $P_-(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,I_2)$. These are complementary rank-two orthogonal projections; the value at this Lebesgue-null point does not change their multiplication operators. Write $M_{P_\pm}$ for their maximal multiplication operators and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}M_{P_\pm}$. The companion matrix lemma on this page proves these are bounded orthogonal projections with closed ranges. The conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ has vectors $\bar u$, scalar multiplication $z\bar u=\overline{\bar z u}$, and pairing $\langle\bar u,\bar v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$.

Use the sine and cosine definitions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. For a length-coordinate increment $t\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix multiplier
$$W_D(t,\mathbf k)=\cos(\omega t)I_4+i\frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega}h_D(\mathbf k).$$
At the massless apex set $W_D(t,0)=I_4$. Its unitarity, group law and generator identity are proved by the companion matrix lemma on this page.

The symbols $P_+$ and $P_-$ designate the positive- and negative-energy matrix formulas for this fixed free Dirac operator. This is purely mathematical data; no physical spin-statistics postulate or empirical assertion is included.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $m>0$ be a particle mass in kilograms, $q\in\mathbb R$ its charge in coulombs, and $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ a smooth spatial vector potential with components in tesla-metres. Set $B_k=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iA_j$ and define on the common core $\mathcal C=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$
$$\pi_i=-i\hbar\partial_i-qA_i,\qquad H_D=c\sum_i\alpha_i\pi_i+\beta mc^2,\qquad \Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i,\sigma_i).$$
Here the matrices are those of [[lem-qft-example-spin-trace-completeness]] and $\hbar,c$ have the SI conventions of [[def-qft-example-data]]. These differential maps preserve $\mathcal C$, and on $\mathcal C$,
$$[\pi_i,\pi_j]=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k,\qquad H_D^2=m^2c^4I_4+c^2(\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B).$$
If the formal first-order square-root coefficient is written as $mc^2+K/(2m)$ with $K=\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B$, then its spin term is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$, where $\mathbf S=\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma/2$. Under the coefficient convention $H_{\mathrm{mag}}=-\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}\cdot\mathbf B$ and $\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}=g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S$, equality of the formal coefficients as a linear function of $q$ gives $g_s=2$ for the minimal tree-level term. No magnetic self-adjoint closure, full spectrum, operator square-root theorem, radiative correction, or empirical prediction is asserted.

citations.quote:
Assume the adopted local Maxwell–Dirac action of
[[post-qft-qed-local-coupling]] with electron charge $q=-e$, $e>0$, and
rest mass $m>0$. Specialize its supplied smooth potential to a static pure
magnetic field on Minkowski space, with $\phi=0$ and
$\mathbf A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in SI units
$\mathrm{T\,m}$. Define $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$ in tesla,
$$ \pi_i=-i\hbar\partial_i-qA_i,\qquad H_D=c\sum_{i=1}^3\alpha_i\pi_i+\beta mc^2, $$
on the common invariant core
$\mathcal D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$. Use the Dirac matrices
and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] and
$$ \Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i,\sigma_i),\qquad S_i=\frac{\hbar}{2}\Sigma_i. $$
The compactly supported spinor-variation Euler–Lagrange equation of the
adopted action, after conversion to SI units, is
$$ i\hbar\partial_t\psi=H_D\psi $$
for this pure magnetic specialization. On $\mathcal D$ its square is
$$ H_D^2=m^2c^4I_4+c^2(\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B). $$
Writing the formal first-order square-root coefficient as
$mc^2+K/(2m)$, where
$K=\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B$, the spin
term is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$. Under the explicitly chosen
magnetic-energy convention
$$ H_{\rm mag}=-\boldsymbol\mu_{\rm mag}\cdot\mathbf B,\qquad \boldsymbol\mu_{\rm mag}=g_s\frac{q}{2m}\mathbf S, $$
coefficient comparison gives $g_s=2$ for this minimal tree coefficient.
The equation is an Euler–Lagrange conclusion, not a claim that every field
is a stationary solution. The square and coefficient are formal on the
stated core; no magnetic self-adjoint closure, full spectrum, radiative
correction, or empirical measurement is asserted.

These are conventions for constructed and formal calculations in this page pair. They are not empirical claims, physical postulates, or existence claims about an interacting continuum theory.

Use the geometric spacetime metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the time coordinate $x^0=ct$ in metres. For Clifford algebra and momentum contraction use the separate algebraic metric $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$; a slash or a square of an energy four-vector uses $h$, never $\eta$.

A physical energy four-vector is $p=(E,c\mathbf p_{\rm phys})$, with each component in joules. Write $M=mc^2$ for rest energy in joules and $p^2=h(p,p)=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p_{\rm phys}|^2$. For two such vectors, $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is in $\mathrm J^2$. Natural momentum coordinates are the energy-vector components divided by $\hbar c$, in $\mathrm m^{-1}$; they are not substituted into SI formulas without restoring this factor. In the common natural-unit field convention, $\mu=mc/\hbar$ is in $\mathrm m^{-1}$, a scalar field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and a Dirac field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$.

Take SI $e>0$ in coulombs, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $c>0$ in metres per second, and $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. Define
$$\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}>0.$$
Here $g$ is a dimensionless coupling. It is not the metric and not a gyromagnetic factor.

For gauge notation set $A_{\rm lower}=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A)$, with $A_a$ in tesla-metres and gauge function $\chi$ in webers. With charge $q$ in coulombs define
$$D_a=\partial_a-\frac{iqA_a}{\hbar},\qquad \psi\mapsto e^{iq\chi/\hbar}\psi,\qquad A\mapsto A+d\chi.$$
For the electron parameter use $q=-e$. The equivalent natural-unit coordinates are $A_{\rm nat}=A_{\rm SI}/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ and $q_{\rm nat}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$.

Finite-matrix examples act on $\mathbb C^d$ with the operator norm. For Hilbert spaces, use the first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=v^\dagger u$; a displayed coordinate contraction $u^\dagger v$ is second-variable-linear and equals $\overline{(u,v)_1}$. Thus norms, traces, and modulus-squared amplitudes agree under conversion, although the unsquared pairing is conjugated. No amplitude is assigned a probability by these conventions.

Use the framework-local unit and domain dictionary of
[[def-qft-framework-units]] and the energy, SI/natural-unit, and finite-matrix
conventions of [[def-qft-example-data]]. A physical quantity is always typed
relative to the selected QFT formulation and its declared model data; its name
or units alone do not identify it with a quantity in another formulation.

For the **exact finite-regulator class** used on this page, the state space is
the finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$ for an integer
$d\ge1$. Model inputs include the selected Hermitian Hamiltonian matrices,
their time-dependent Hermitian interaction when present, a dimensionless
coupling parameter, an initial state, and an explicitly supplied finite
outcome measurement. A pure initial state is a vector $\psi\in\mathbb C^d$
with $\|\psi\|=1$; a mixed state is a matrix $\rho=\rho^*$ with
$\langle\rho v,v\rangle\ge0$ for every $v$ and $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$.
An exact regulated observable on this finite space is a specified Hermitian
matrix $O=O^*$ with a declared physical unit. The matrix and state are model
data; the measurement procedure and any physical rule assigning outcomes are
additional data. This definition does not say that an operator symbol by
itself is a detector outcome or probability.

A **finite probability law** on the declared outcome set
$\{1,\ldots,m\}$, $m\ge1$, is a vector $(p_1,\ldots,p_m)$ with
$p_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a=1}^m p_a=1$. It is a mathematical type. Assigning that
law to a particular preparation and measurement is a separate physical
postulate. A prediction derived from an actually constructed regulated model
is conditional on those inputs and the adopted rule.

A **formal coefficient record** is a sequence $(c_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of
specified coefficients, sometimes displayed as the symbol
$\sum_{n\ge0}c_n\lambda^n$. Unless convergence and an evaluation map are
separately proved and adopted, the symbol records coefficients only: it is not
an evaluated function, exact probability, convergent perturbation series, or
error bound. A formal coefficient can be assigned a phenomenological meaning
only by a separate, model-specific physical adoption with its approximation
scope stated.

An **empirical estimate** is a source-reported number obtained by analyzing a
finite record of measurement outcomes under the stated preparation, apparatus,
calibration, sampling, and analysis conditions. Its reported uncertainty and
conditions travel with the estimate. It is not the exact model value, and it
does not prove the framework used to interpret it. The 2022 Fan et al. report
is an example of a source-reported electron magnetic-moment determination;
this definition supplies no numerical result, uncertainty reconstruction, or
new experimental claim.

Primitive and derived status is formulation-relative. In a selected regulated
model, the regulator, Hamiltonian data, coupling, initial state, and supplied
measurement are declared inputs; an evolution, amplitude, or probability law
is derived only when the construction and adopted rule establish it. In a
formal calculation, the specified masses, couplings, coefficient rules, and
subtraction prescription are inputs, while its listed coefficients are
derived within that formal calculation. An empirical estimate is a reported
data-analysis result, not a primitive model parameter or a theorem.

The following units are examples of types, not identifications of quantities:
a cross section $\sigma$ is area-valued with SI unit $\mathrm{m^2}$; a rate
$\Gamma$ is inverse-time-valued with unit $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$; an energy width
$\Gamma_E$ has unit joule. Only a separately stated convention may identify
$\Gamma_E=\hbar\Gamma$. The fine-structure parameter $\alpha$, a dimensionless
coupling $g$, and a gyromagnetic factor $g_s$ are dimensionless but have
different physical meanings. The name “width,” a common symbol, or matching
dimensions does not supply an exponential-decay law or an equality between
these parameters.

facts.text: [F1] [[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $V_\lambda(q)\ge(m^2/2)q^2$, so $C_0=0$ and the common quadratic coercivity constant is $c=m^2/2$.

facts.label: F2
facts.text:
[F2] [[lem-qft-hermite-oscillator-research-supplier]]: with $c=m^2/2$, the oscillator form domain $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the $\lambda=0$ form domain $Q_0$, the completion for the shifted norm $a\|u'\|_2^2+\int((m^2/2)q^2+2)|u|^2\,dq$. Its complete orthonormal Hermite basis has energies $\epsilon_n=(2n+1)m\sqrt{a/2}$ and, for every $u\in Q_0$, the exact form expansion
$$q_0(u)=a\|u'\|_2^2+\frac{m^2}{2}\|qu\|_2^2=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\epsilon_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The normalized ground function $\psi_0(q)=\phi_b(q)=(b/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-bq^2/2}$, with $b=m/\sqrt{2a}$, belongs to $Q_0$.

facts.label: F3

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: if measurable functions $f_n$ converge almost everywhere to $f$ and satisfy $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for one nonnegative $g$ with finite integral, then $\int f_n\to\int f$. The proof below supplies this pointwise convergence and an integrable majorant for the Gaussian difference quotients.

facts.label: F6

facts.label: F7
facts.text:
[F7] For a real function continuous on a closed interval $[u,v]$, $u<v$,
and differentiable on $(u,v)$, the difference quotient equals a derivative

steps.text: Write $a_\lambda=q_\lambda+2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ for the shifted form inner product of the $\lambda$ completion. On $C_c^\infty$, $V_\lambda\ge V_0$ gives $a_\lambda(u,u)\ge a_0(u,u)$, so a $Q_\lambda$-Cauchy sequence is $Q_0$-Cauchy and the identity extends continuously to $Q_\lambda\to Q_0$ with the same $L^2$ representative. The unshifted forms $q_\lambda=a_\lambda-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ and $q_0=a_0-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ are continuous on their respective form spaces. For any $u\in Q_\lambda$, approximate it in $Q_\lambda$ by $u_r\in C_c^\infty$; then $q_\lambda(u_r)\ge q_0(u_r)$ for every $r$, and continuity of both forms gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)$ in the limit. For normalized $u\in Q_\lambda$, [F3] then gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)\ge E_g(0)$. Taking the infimum yields $E_g(\lambda)\ge E_g(0)$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

steps.text:
Write $p_b(q):=\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2}$ and $\mathbb E_b[g]:=\int g(q)p_b(q)\,dq$. For $g\in\{1,q^2\}$, the real-valued integrand has derivative in $b$
$$\partial_b(g(q)p_b(q))=g(q)\left(\frac1{2b}-q^2\right)p_b(q).$$
Fix $b_0>0$ and choose a compact interval $K=[b_0-\delta,b_0+\delta]\subset(0,\infty)$; put $b_*:=b_0-\delta$. There is a constant $C_K$ such that, for both choices of $g$ and every $s\in K$,
$$|\partial_s(g(q)p_s(q))|\le C_K(1+|q|^4)e^{-b_*q^2},$$
and the right side is integrable on $\mathbb R$. For any sequence of nonzero $h_r\to0$ with $b_0+h_r\in K$, for each fixed $q$ and $g\in\{1,q^2\}$ the function
$s\mapsto g(q)p_s(q)$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$, hence continuous on the
closed interval between $b_0$ and $b_0+h_r$ and differentiable in its
interior. This interval is contained in $K$ and has distinct endpoints.
Thus [F7] bounds the difference quotients
$$\left|\frac{g(q)p_{b_0+h_r}(q)-g(q)p_{b_0}(q)}{h_r}\right|\le C_K(1+|q|^4)e^{-b_*q^2};$$
they converge pointwise to $\partial_b(g(q)p_b(q))|_{b=b_0}$. Applying [F5] to these quotients gives convergence of their integrals to the integral of that derivative. Since this holds for every such sequence, it proves for each $b_0>0$ that
$$\frac{d}{db}\mathbb E_b[g]\bigg|_{b=b_0}=\int_{\mathbb R}\partial_b(g(q)p_b(q))\big|_{b=b_0}\,dq.$$
Thus [F5] is used only after the local difference-quotient convergence and majorant have been established. Since $\mathbb E_b[1]=1$, differentiating gives
$$0=\mathbb E_b\!\left[\frac1{2b}-q^2\right],\qquad \mathbb E_b[q^2]=\frac1{2b}.$$
Differentiating this identity for $\mathbb E_b[q^2]$ gives
$$-\frac1{2b^2}=\mathbb E_b\!\left[q^2\left(\frac1{2b}-q^2\right)\right] =\frac1{4b^2}-\mathbb E_b[q^4],$$
so $\mathbb E_b[q^4]=3/(4b^2)$. Since $\phi_b'=-bq\phi_b$, it follows that
$$\|\phi_b\|_2^2=1,\quad \|\phi_b'\|_2^2=b/2,\quad \int q^2|\phi_b|^2=1/(2b),\quad\int q^4|\phi_b|^2=3/(4b^2).$$
[F2, F5, F7, algebra]

Put $\epsilon_0:=m\sqrt{a/2}$. For every $u\in Q_0$, the exact expansion in [F2], together with $\epsilon_n\ge\epsilon_0$ and Parseval from [F6] for its complete orthonormal basis, gives
$$q_0(u)-\epsilon_0\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(\epsilon_n-\epsilon_0)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2\ge0.$$
The normalized $\phi_b=\psi_0\in Q_0$ has only its ground coefficient nonzero, so [F2] also gives $q_0(\phi_b)=\epsilon_0$. In particular the moment calculation of step 1.3 yields
$$a\|\phi_b'\|_2^2+\frac{m^2}{2}\|q\phi_b\|_2^2=\frac{ab}{2}+\frac{m^2}{4b}=m\sqrt{\frac a2}=\epsilon_0,$$
where $b=m/\sqrt{2a}$. Hence the normalized form infimum for $q_0$ is $\epsilon_0$, and the variational-bound lemma [F3] identifies this infimum with $E_g(0)$; therefore $E_g(0)=\epsilon_0$. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.3, algebra]
