citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). A **finite-mode regulator** in this item is a fixed
finite nonempty label set $J$ with $N:=|J|\ge1$, a fixed enumeration of $J$ by
$\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and the real coordinate vector
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may name sites of a finite
lattice or finitely many modes; their geometry enters only through the chosen
polynomial below. No limit in $N$ is part of this definition.

Choose real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$, constants $c>0$ and $C_0\ge0$,
and a real polynomial $V\in\mathbb R[q_1,\ldots,q_N]$ such that
$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$
Let $H_N:=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with vectors identified up to almost
everywhere equality and inner product
$$\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}u(q)\overline{v(q)}\,dq,$$
linear in the first variable. Under Countable Choice this is a complex Hilbert
space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let
$D_0:=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, the smooth compactly supported
complex-valued functions. The associated **polynomial differential expression**
is the map
$$h_0:D_0\to H_N,\qquad h_0u:=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Vu.$$
It is well defined because each derivative of $u$ and the product $Vu$ are
smooth and compactly supported. Set $W:=V+C_0+1$, so
$W(q)\ge1+c|q|^2$. This definition specifies finite mathematical data and a
differential expression; it does not choose a self-adjoint operator domain or
assert a continuum or infinite-volume limit.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.

Assume Countable Choice and use $Q$, $q_h$, and the operator $h$ from
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let $\lambda_1$ be the least
eigenvalue of $h$. Then
$$\inf\{q_h(u):u\in Q,\ \|u\|_2=1\}=\lambda_1.$$
The infimum is attained by every normalized vector in the lowest eigenspace;
no simplicity or nondegeneracy is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Write $a_\lambda=q_\lambda+2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ for the shifted form inner product of the $\lambda$ completion. facts.label: A1
facts.text:
[A1] Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as required for the
Hilbert-adjoint definition used here.

facts.label: F1
facts.text:
[F1] A complex Hilbert space is complete in its norm ([[def-hilbert-space]]);
$\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ is the space of bounded linear operators and
$\|\cdot\|$ is their operator norm
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]], [[def-operator-norm]]).

facts.label: F2
facts.text:
[F2] The Hilbert adjoint is characterized by the inner-product identity, and
for a bounded operator self-adjoint means equality with that adjoint
([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

facts.label: A2
facts.text:
[A2] $V(t)$ is strongly continuous, self-adjoint at each $t$, and
uniformly bounded by $M$ on $I$. Strong continuity means that
$t\mapsto V(t)\psi$ is norm-continuous for every $\psi$.

facts.label: A3
facts.text:
[A3] For the factorization clause, $V_1,V_2$ satisfy the same hypotheses
and are supported in the strictly ordered time intervals $[d,b]$ and
$[a,c]$, respectively, with $c<d$.

facts.label: F3
facts.text:
[F3] A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space is
bounded ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

facts.label: F4
facts.text:
[F4] The complex exponential is given by its power series, and
$\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$ converges absolutely for every $z\in\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]).

facts.label: F5
facts.text:
[F5] Continuous scalar functions on compact intervals are Riemann integrable,
and integrating a continuous derivative gives its endpoint difference
([[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]],
[[thm-ftc-second-part]]).

facts.label: F6
facts.text:
[F6] The derivative of a polynomial follows the ordinary product rule
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

facts.label: F7
facts.text:
[F7] A continuous map from a compact metric space to any metric space is
uniformly continuous. [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]

steps.text:
If $a=b$, every integral is zero, $U_0=I$, and $U_n=0$ for $n\ge1$; all evolution and unitarity claims follow, while no $c<d$ lies in $I$, so the separated-support clause has no instance. Assume henceforth $a<b$. Suppose $U_n(r,s)\psi$ is continuous in $r$. For fixed $r_0$, $$ \|V(r)U_n(r,s)\psi-V(r_0)U_n(r_0,s)\psi\| \le M\|U_n(r,s)\psi-U_n(r_0,s)\psi\| +\|(V(r)-V(r_0))U_n(r_0,s)\psi\|, $$ which tends to zero by strong continuity of $V$. Thus the recursive integrand is continuous. Apply [F7] to the compact interval $I=[a,b]$ with metric $|r-r'|$
and the Hilbert space with norm metric $\|u-v\|$. The preceding estimate
proves continuity of $r\mapsto V(r)U_n(r,s)\psi$ for each fixed $s,\psi$,
so [F7] gives its uniform continuity. Its vector-valued Riemann integral
therefore exists: this uniform continuity makes the tagged sums for the explicit equal-mesh partitions Cauchy; completeness of $\mathcal H$ gives their limit. Uniform continuity also bounds the difference between sums on any two sufficiently fine tagged partitions by a quantity tending to zero, so this limit is independent of the partitions and tags. The tagged-sum triangle inequality, followed by the scalar Riemann-sum limit from [F5], gives $\|\int f\|\le\int\|f\|$. The integral as a function of its upper endpoint is continuous, since its increment has norm at most the interval length times the supremum of the continuous integrand; this supremum is finite by [F3]. This proves strong continuity of $U_{n+1}(\cdot,s)\psi$ and closes the induction. [A2, F1, F3, F5, F7, construct]

steps.text: The identity operator has norm at most one, including when $\mathcal H=\{0\}$. The integral estimate then gives inductively $$ \|U_{n+1}(t,s)\| \le\int_{\min(s,t)}^{\max(s,t)}M\frac{M^n|r-s|^n}{n!}\,dr =\frac{M^{n+1}|t-s|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}. $$ This proves the factorial bound for both orientations of the integral. [step 1.1, F1, A2, F5, F6, algebra]

The integral estimate then gives inductively $$ \|U_{n+1}(t,s)\| \le\int_{\min(s,t)}^{\max(s,t)}M\frac{M^n|r-s|^n}{n!}\,dr =\frac{M^{n+1}|t-s|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}. $$ This proves the factorial bound for both orientations of the integral.

steps.text: The bound in step 2.1 makes $\sum z^nU_n(t,s)$ absolutely and uniformly convergent in operator norm on $I^2$, with total norm at most $\sum_{n\ge0}(|z|M(b-a))^n/n!=e^{|z|M(b-a)}$ by [F4]. The recursion and this uniform bound permit termwise integration on each vector: the norm of the integral of a uniform tail is at most $(b-a)$ times its supremum norm, which tends to zero. This gives the displayed integral equation. [A2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

The recursion and this uniform bound permit termwise integration on each vector: the norm of the integral of a uniform tail is at most $(b-a)$ times its supremum norm, which tends to zero. This gives the displayed integral equation.

steps.text: If $X(t,s)$ and $Y(t,s)$ are two strongly continuous solutions, then for fixed $\psi$, $D(t)=\|(X(t,s)-Y(t,s))\psi\|$ is bounded on $I$ by [F3] and is Riemann integrable by [F5]. It satisfies $D(t)\le |z|M\int_{\min(s,t)}^{\max(s,t)}D(r)\,dr$. Repeated substitution gives an $n$-fold integral over the ordered simplex between $s$ and $t$; induction using [F5] and the polynomial derivative rule [F6] evaluates its volume as $|t-s|^n/n!$, so $$ D(t)\le C_\psi\frac{(|z|M|t-s|)^n}{n!} $$ with $C_\psi=\sup_{r\in I}D(r)<\infty$. The right side tends to zero, so the solution is unique. To prove composition, split the equation for $U_z(t,s)$ at $r$: for $t\ge r$, it reads $U_z(t,s)=U_z(r,s)-iz\int_r^tV(q)U_z(q,s)\,dq$. Multiplying the equation for $U_z(t,r)$ on the right by $U_z(r,s)$ shows $U_z(t,r)U_z(r,s)$ solves this same initial-value equation and has the same value at $t=r$. The uniqueness estimate just proved, with initial time $r$, gives equality; the reversed orientation proves it for $t<r$. [step 3.1, A2, F3, F5, F6, algebra]

steps.text: For a continuous vector-valued integrand, the average over a signed interval of length $h$ converges in norm to its value at the base point: the error is bounded by the supremum of its variation on that interval. Taking difference quotients in the integral equation therefore gives $\partial_tU_z(t,s)\psi=-izV(t)U_z(t,s)\psi$. If $u(t)=U_z(t,s)\psi$, then $$ \frac{\|u(t+h)\|^2-\|u(t)\|^2}{h} =2\operatorname{Re}\left\langle u(t),\frac{u(t+h)-u(t)}h\right\rangle +\frac{\|u(t+h)-u(t)\|^2}{h}. $$ The second term tends to zero and the first tends to $2\operatorname{Re}\langle u(t),-izV(t)u(t)\rangle=0$ for real $z$, because self-adjointness makes $\langle u,V(t)u\rangle$ real. Thus $U_z(t,s)$ is an isometry. [A1, F1, F2, A2, step 3.1, algebra]

steps.text: By the composition law in step 4.1, $U_z(t,s)U_z(s,t)=U_z(t,t)=I_{\mathcal H}$ and $U_z(s,t)U_z(t,s)=U_z(s,s)=I_{\mathcal H}$. Hence $U_z(t,s)$ is surjective. Step 4.2 shows that it is an isometry when $z$ is real. By the unitary convention stated above, $U_z(t,s)$ is unitary. [step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

steps.text: Let $Y(t)=U_z^{V_1}(t,a)U_z^{V_2}(t,a)$. For each $\psi$, $$ \frac{Y(t+h)\psi-Y(t)\psi}{h} =\frac{U_z^{V_1}(t+h,a)-U_z^{V_1}(t,a)}{h}U_z^{V_2}(t+h,a)\psi +U_z^{V_1}(t,a)\frac{U_z^{V_2}(t+h,a)-U_z^{V_2}(t,a)}{h}\psi. $$ Strong continuity, the local operator bounds, and the differential equations from step 4.2 make the right side converge to the product-rule derivative. Before the later support interval, $U_z^{V_1}(t,a)=I$; after the earlier support interval, $U_z^{V_2}(t,a)$ is constant. Thus on the earlier interval, the gap, and the later interval, this derivative is $\partial_tY=-iz(V_1(t)+V_2(t))Y$, and $Y(a)=I$. Integrating across the three regions and using continuity at their endpoints shows that $Y$ solves the integral equation for $V_1+V_2$. Uniqueness from step 4.1 yields the stated factorization at $b$. Both sides have operator-norm-convergent power series for every $z$. Their equality for all real $z$ forces equality of coefficients: if a first coefficient differed, divide the difference by its least power of $z$ and let real $z\to0$, contradicting the equality. [A2, A3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra, algebra] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. Write

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Repeated substitution gives an $n$-fold integral over the ordered simplex between $s$ and $t$; induction using [F5] and the polynomial derivative rule [F6] evaluates its volume as $|t-s|^n/n!$, so $$ D(t)\le C_\psi\frac{(|z|M|t-s|)^n}{n!} $$ with $C_\psi=\sup_{r\in I}D(r)<\infty$. The right side tends to zero, so the solution is unique. To prove composition, split the equation for $U_z(t,s)$ at $r$: for $t\ge r$, it reads $U_z(t,s)=U_z(r,s)-iz\int_r^tV(q)U_z(q,s)\,dq$. Multiplying the equation for $U_z(t,r)$ on the right by $U_z(r,s)$ shows $U_z(t,r)U_z(r,s)$ solves this same initial-value equation and has the same value at $t=r$. The uniqueness estimate just proved, with initial time $r$, gives equality; the reversed orientation proves it for $t<r$.

For a continuous vector-valued integrand, the average over a signed interval of length $h$ converges in norm to its value at the base point: the error is bounded by the supremum of its variation on that interval. Taking difference quotients in the integral equation therefore gives $\partial_tU_z(t,s)\psi=-izV(t)U_z(t,s)\psi$. If $u(t)=U_z(t,s)\psi$, then $$ \frac{\|u(t+h)\|^2-\|u(t)\|^2}{h} =2\operatorname{Re}\left\langle u(t),\frac{u(t+h)-u(t)}h\right\rangle +\frac{\|u(t+h)-u(t)\|^2}{h}. $$ The second term tends to zero and the first tends to $2\operatorname{Re}\langle u(t),-izV(t)u(t)\rangle=0$ for real $z$, because self-adjointness makes $\langle u,V(t)u\rangle$ real. Thus $U_z(t,s)$ is an isometry.

By the composition law in step 4.1, $U_z(t,s)U_z(s,t)=U_z(t,t)=I_{\mathcal H}$ and $U_z(s,t)U_z(t,s)=U_z(s,s)=I_{\mathcal H}$. Hence $U_z(t,s)$ is surjective. Step 4.2 shows that it is an isometry when $z$ is real. By the unitary convention stated above, $U_z(t,s)$ is unitary.

Let $Y(t)=U_z^{V_1}(t,a)U_z^{V_2}(t,a)$. For each $\psi$, $$ \frac{Y(t+h)\psi-Y(t)\psi}{h} =\frac{U_z^{V_1}(t+h,a)-U_z^{V_1}(t,a)}{h}U_z^{V_2}(t+h,a)\psi +U_z^{V_1}(t,a)\frac{U_z^{V_2}(t+h,a)-U_z^{V_2}(t,a)}{h}\psi. $$ Strong continuity, the local operator bounds, and the differential equations from step 4.2 make the right side converge to the product-rule derivative. Before the later support interval, $U_z^{V_1}(t,a)=I$; after the earlier support interval, $U_z^{V_2}(t,a)$ is constant. Thus on the earlier interval, the gap, and the later interval, this derivative is $\partial_tY=-iz(V_1(t)+V_2(t))Y$, and $Y(a)=I$. Integrating across the three regions and using continuity at their endpoints shows that $Y$ solves the integral equation for $V_1+V_2$. Uniqueness from step 4.1 yields the stated factorization at $b$. Both sides have operator-norm-convergent power series for every $z$. Their equality for all real $z$ forces equality of coefficients: if a first coefficient differed, divide the difference by its least power of $z$ and let real $z\to0$, contradicting the equality.

facts.text: [F1] [[def-qft-quartic-graph-power-counting]]: the internal-edge ends and the attached external half-edges are in bijection with the four incidence slots at each vertex; $L:=I-V+1$ is the cycle rank; one formal loop integration contributes degree $D$, each internal scalar propagator contributes degree $-2$, and $\omega_D(\Gamma):=DL-2I$. steps.text: Counting the four slots at every vertex gives $4V$ slots. Each of the $I$ internal edges occupies two slots, including a self-loop, and each of the $E$ external half-edges occupies one. Hence $4V=2I+E$. [given, F1, algebra]

steps.text: Start with one vertex and repeatedly add an internal edge from the reached vertices to a vertex not yet reached. Connectedness provides such an edge until all $V$ vertices are reached. Exactly $I-(V-1)=I-V+1=L$ internal edges lie outside this tree, including any unselected loops or parallel edges, so the cycle rank in [F1] is nonnegative and counts the non-tree internal edges. citations.quote: A **finite quartic graph** is a finite connected multigraph $\Gamma$ with $V\ge1$ vertices, each having exactly four incidence slots. An internal edge uses two slots, including a self-loop at one vertex; parallel internal edges are allowed. An **external half-edge** uses one slot and has no paired endpoint. Let $I$ be the number of internal edges and $E$ the number of external half-edges. Define the **loop count** (the graph's cycle rank) by $$L:=I-V+1.$$ For this mathematical power-counting convention, assign degree $D$ to each independent loop-momentum integration over $\mathbb R^D$, degree $-2$ to each internal scalar propagator, and degree $0$ to each quartic vertex. The propagator assignment is its leading ultraviolet degree under a common dilation of loop momenta; for example, a Euclidean scalar factor $(|q|^2+m^2)^{-1}$ with $m\ge0$ is assigned degree $-2$. The **superficial degree** of $\Gamma$ is $$\omega_D(\Gamma):=DL-2I.$$ By convention, $\omega_D(\Gamma)=0$ is called a **logarithmic superficial degree**. This is finite graph bookkeeping under the stated assignment. It does not by itself establish convergence or divergence of an actual graph integral; proper subgraphs, numerator cancellations, exceptional infrared data, and distributional singularities require separate hypotheses and analysis.

Substitute L=I−V+1 and I=2V−E/2 into the defining degree DL−2I and simplify to D+(D−4)V−(D−2)E/2.
Set D=4 in the general formula to obtain ω4=4−E and retain the definition’s superficial-only interpretation.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the finite-regulator
spectral and trace construction. For the fixed model of
[[post-qft-regulated-polynomial-model]] and a declared
temperature input $T>0$, use
[[def-qft-regulated-thermal-parameter]] to set
$\beta_{\rm phys}=(k_BT)^{-1}$ and
$\widehat\beta=E_*\beta_{\rm phys}>0$. Let $h$ be the model's specified
self-adjoint form realization and $H_{\rm phys}=E_*h$. When the finite-mode
coercivity hypotheses hold, [[thm-qft-regulated-gibbs-trace]] proves that
$e^{-\widehat\beta h}$ is positive trace class with finite positive trace.
Adopt the normalized operator

$$\rho_T:=\frac{e^{-\beta_{\rm phys}H_{\rm phys}}}{Z_T},\qquad Z_T:=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta_{\rm phys}H_{\rm phys}})$$

as this finite-regulator model's canonical equilibrium state. This is a
physical state assignment, not a deduction that the dynamics reach
equilibrium. It asserts no infinite-volume trace, no zero-temperature state,
and no empirical observation.

Adopt the following physical reading only for an explicitly selected model
whose mathematical data have actually been constructed. Let $\mathscr H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $\rho_t$ be the model's density operator at
a time $t$ at which a measurement is made, and let
$\{M_{a,r}:r=1,\ldots,q_a\}_{a=1}^m$ be a supplied normalized finite bounded
Kraus instrument on $\mathscr H$ in the exact sense of
[[def-qft-finite-bounded-kraus-instrument]]. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ when using the normalization result of
[[lem-qft-finite-instrument-normalization]]. Its hypotheses include that
$\rho_t$ is a density operator and that the instrument really satisfies
$\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_{\mathscr H}$; the supplier's result is a draft
with a complete conditional proof, not an independent approval or an
apparatus-realization theorem.

Put

$$E_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad
\mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_rM_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*.$$

As the **Born interpretation postulate** for this selected model, read

$$p_a(t):=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho_t))
=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_tE_a)$$

as the model probability for outcome $a$. The mathematical supplier proves
$p_a(t)\in[0,1]$ and $\sum_{a=1}^mp_a(t)=1$ under the hypotheses just
listed. When $p_a(t)>0$, adopt
$\mathcal J_a(\rho_t)/p_a(t)$ as the model's conditional state after outcome
$a$; at zero probability no normalized update is assigned. These are
model-level probability assignments, not observations.

If the selected construction supplies a self-adjoint observable in the sense
of [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]] and its
spectral projection-valued measure as in
[[def-projection-valued-measure]], a declared finite Borel partition may be
used only after its projections have been constructed and verified as a
finite projective instrument. In that case the projections are the single
Kraus operators for their outcomes. A supplied bounded effect is read as an
outcome effect only as part of a supplied normalized instrument; this item
does not construct square roots, a spectral measure, or an instrument from an
arbitrary formal observable.

If a model has actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $\widehat H$
and its unitary evolution, adopt the Schrödinger convention
$U(t)=\exp(-it\widehat H/\hbar)$ and
$\rho_t=U(t)\rho_0U(t)^*$ when that construction establishes that $\rho_t$
is a density operator. In the Heisenberg representation use
$O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. This postulate neither constructs the Hamiltonian,
unitary group, state, field representation, nor their domains.

The model declaration identifies the selected species, field normalization,
regulator, preparation and measurement data using
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. It does not assert that every classical action
has a quantization, that every formal state is positive, or that any cutoff
can be removed. In particular it supplies no interacting continuum
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, scattering operator, asymptotic
completeness, LSZ limit, or nonperturbative convergence. A formal coefficient
is not an exact probability without an additional controlled approximation
map and a constructed model. Agreement with reported data would test the
selected approximation and empirical inputs; it would not prove this
postulate or the model. No reported data are asserted here.

Assume Countable Choice and use the finite-mode data, form domain $Q$, and
self-adjoint $h$ from [[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let
$\lambda_0\le\lambda_1\le\cdots$ be its eigenvalues repeated with
multiplicity, and let $\psi_k$ be a corresponding orthonormal eigenbasis. For
$\beta>0$ define the finite-rank truncations
$$\rho_{\beta,M}f:=\sum_{k=0}^M e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\psi_k.$$
The proof establishes their operator-norm limit $\rho_\beta$, with action
$$\rho_\beta f:=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\psi_k.$$
Put $\alpha_j:=\sqrt{a_jc}$ and let the oscillator eigenvalues
$\epsilon_k$ be the nondecreasing ordering, with multiplicity, of
$$\epsilon_{\mathbf n}=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\alpha_j, \qquad\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N.$$
Then $\rho_\beta$ is positive trace class and its trace
$$Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta)=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}$$
satisfies the finite bound
$$0<Z_\beta\le e^{\beta C_0} \prod_{j=1}^N\frac{e^{-\beta\alpha_j}}{1-e^{-2\beta\alpha_j}}<\infty.$$
For every bounded linear operator $B:H_N\to H_N$, the normalized trace
expectation is well defined and
$$Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B) =Z_\beta^{-1}\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k} \langle B\psi_k,\psi_k\rangle,$$
with absolute convergence. This is a finite-$N$ mathematical trace result;
it assumes no statistical data and makes no continuum-limit claim.

For the fixed model of [[post-qft-regulated-polynomial-model]], use the SI
energy-unit convention of [[def-qft-framework-units]]. A declared temperature
input is a scalar $T>0$ with unit kelvin (K). Take $k_B>0$, with
unit $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, as the fixed Boltzmann conversion constant in this
branch. Define the physical inverse-energy parameter

$$\beta_{\rm phys}:=\frac{1}{k_BT}\quad[\mathrm{J^{-1}}],$$

and its dimensionless form

$$\widehat\beta:=E_*\beta_{\rm phys}.$$

The product $k_BT$ has unit joule, and $\widehat\beta$ is dimensionless
because $E_*$ has unit joule. Since $k_B>0$ and $T>0$, both inverse parameters
are defined and positive. The values of $T$ and the model's choice of $k_B$
are inputs; this definition does not infer them from a state or an
experiment. It defines a parameter convention only and asserts no dynamical
thermalization.

citations.quote: **(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every $p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive diagonal entries.
An orientation of an $n$-manifold is a smooth choice of a ray in $\det T_pM$ for every $p$.

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector $n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$.
$\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite.

**(a) Congruences.** An **observer congruence** on $U$ is a smooth vector field $n$ on $U$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) such that $n_q$ is an observer at $q$ for every $q\in U$ ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]); explicitly, $$g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1\quad\text{and}\quad g_q(n_q,N_q)<0\qquad\text{for every }q\in U .$$ Since $g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1$, the field $n$ is nowhere vanishing.

**(c) Tetrad fields.** A **tetrad field** (or **$g$-orthonormal frame field**) on $U$ is a local frame field $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ on $U$ such that $$g_q(E_A(q),E_B(q))=\eta_{AB}\qquad\text{for all }A,B\text{ and all }q\in U .$$ A tetrad field is **future-directed** when in addition $E_0(q)$ is future-directed for every $q\in U$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]); then each $E_0(q)$ is an observer at $q$ ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]), so $E_0$ is an observer congruence on $U$ ([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]), while $E_1,E_2,E_3$ are pointwise an orthonormal basis of the rest space of that observer.
**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for $(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and $g$-compatible.

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]), $$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$ on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and $$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$ For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with $$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement.

facts.label: F3

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.
